## Acting Before Resolution

A [[decision|Decision]] may be required before its consequences are known. Its [[significance|Significance]] depends partly on who bears those consequences and whether a mistake can be corrected. Choosing to wait for greater confidence can also have consequences when delay changes the available possibilities. A late caregiver may still be on the way. A person who needs help by a particular time can make a [[making-a-backup-arrangement|backup arrangement]] while the reason for the delay is still unknown. If a neighbor who can give a ride needs ten minutes to get ready, the time to call comes before the time to leave. Waiting until the missed visit is certain may leave too little time to use the ride.

In describing [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]], distinguish uncertainty faced by a person at the time from uncertainty faced by an observer afterward. An outcome alone does not tell us what someone could reasonably have expected.

A provisional decision can name what would justify revisiting it: a new observation, a changed consequence, or a failed [[expectation|Expectation]]. A failed expectation warrants examining what was expected, what was observed, and how they were compared; it does not by itself establish which alternative explanation is correct. This makes uncertainty specific enough to examine without pretending that every unsettled question can be resolved before action.

events.title: Expectation
events.summary: Ask how to assess a prediction when the person who made it also brought about the outcome.
events.body: What if the expectation helps bring about the outcome? Suppose I write that I expect the door to be locked by six, then go and lock it myself. The note is evidence of what I said beforehand. To judge my grounds, it matters whether I already planned to lock it or only decided to later. Could the last paragraph make room for that distinction?

events.title: Regret
events.summary: Extend the route example to distinguish what someone learned afterward from what they could have known when choosing.
events.body:
Regret is an unfavorable judgment about something that happened, accompanied by a wish that it had been otherwise. It may concern an action, an omission, or a circumstance beyond the person’s control. Regretting an outcome does not by itself establish responsibility for it.

An alternative choice and its imagined result are two different things. Someone may know they could have taken another route while remaining uncertain whether it would have got them there sooner. An account should distinguish what occurred, what the person knew at the time, and what they now believe might have happened. Later knowledge does not automatically make an earlier [[decision|decision]] unreasonable. In the route example, learning afterward that a road was closed is different from finding out there was a closure notice at the turn. The notice bears on what the person could reasonably have known before choosing.

As part of [[human-experience|Human Experience]], regret raises questions about the [[significance|Significance]] assigned to lost possibilities. Its intensity does not by itself establish the extent of a loss or its consequences; the experience of regret may nevertheless be significant to the person. For understanding [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]], a further distinction matters: wishing to undo a past choice is different from deciding what to do next. [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]] can remain in both judgments.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Specify what the shared list prevents and use the grocery example to show how a recipient can change or decline the arrangement.
events.body:
Two neighbors each leave a bag of groceries by the same door. Each bought what was on the list, and someone now has to find room for two cartons of milk. When people arrange help separately, the overlap may become apparent only after they have spent the time or money.

Overlapping help can be deliberate, as in [[making-a-backup-arrangement|Making a Backup Arrangement]], where one person is asked to be available if another cannot come. In the grocery example, both people understood that they were being asked to shop. A shared list that records who has taken each item can help prevent duplicate purchases. It can also give the person receiving [[care|care]] another thing to keep up to date, depending on who is expected to mark the list.

The list can settle who buys the milk while leaving open whether the person wants groceries left at the door. If they ask for a pickup instead, the neighbors may need to change the arrangement before either shops. If the person wants to shop for themselves, [[declining-help|declining help]] may mean taking the list out of use altogether.

events.title: Social Organization
events.summary: Offer replacement text that keeps the deadline, delivery delay, and clerk in the overview.
events.body: Suggested replacement for the Access to Review section: Suppose a housing office hears objections only if it receives them within ten days of sending a notice. A delay in delivery gives the recipient less time to respond. The clerk who records the receipt date and applies the deadline can determine whether a reviewer ever sees the objection. The procedure for contesting a finding of lateness is a question of [[access-to-review|Access to Review]].

events.title: Habit
events.summary: Suggest stating how the arrangement is known in the gate example.
events.body: The gate example fits if the arrangement is known independently of the locked gate. If all we know is that the gate was locked once, the neighbor’s absence is one possible explanation. If we already know the gate is left open for the bins, we can check the narrower description on other Thursdays when the neighbor is due.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Show how a refusal reaches both neighbors when they arranged the shopping separately.
events.body:

It can also give the person receiving [[care|care]] another thing to keep up to date, depending on who is expected to mark the list.

The list can settle who buys the milk while leaving open whether the person wants groceries left at the door. events.title: Care
events.summary: Extend the shift example to distinguish reporting a delayed handover from transferring responsibility for care.
events.body:
Care is attention and activity directed toward someone's needs or well-being. Preparing a meal, remembering an appointment, or accompanying someone are ordinary activities through which care can be examined. Describing them involves asking what is needed, who notices, who acts, and whose account of the need is heard.

## Care and Arrangements

Care connects [[attention|Attention]] with the distribution of obligations in [[social-organization|Social Organization]]. Performing a task and remaining available to perform it are distinct responsibilities. An account concerned only with completed tasks may leave that availability undescribed. Availability can take the form of [[waiting|Waiting]]: having no immediate task while being unable to leave. Describing such an arrangement involves asking when responsibility ends and who can take it over. An empty task list does not answer either question.

A shift rule can make relief depend on an acknowledgment from the incoming worker. In a care setting with such a rule, the outgoing worker may have finished every scheduled task and still have to stay until someone accepts responsibility. If the incoming worker has arrived but is occupied elsewhere, the rule makes arrival alone insufficient. The person who can acknowledge the [[handing-over-care|handover]] also determines when the outgoing worker is free to leave.

A second rule may specify what happens when nobody acknowledges the handover. If the outgoing worker must call a supervisor after fifteen minutes, the call brings the delay to someone who can arrange relief. The worker remains responsible until a replacement accepts the handover, unless the rule also authorizes the supervisor to take responsibility directly. A record of the call can therefore show that the worker asked for relief while leaving open who was responsible for care during the wait.

Calling an activity care does not establish that it is wanted or effective. The intention of the person providing it and the [[human-experience|Human Experience]] of the person receiving it are separate matters. Where they differ, describing the disagreement is more informative than allowing the label to settle it. An account can also ask what the recipient must do: explain a need, repeat an instruction, or make room for help. These activities belong to the description of care as well as the task performed.

The everyday character of care does not determine its [[significance|Significance]]. A small activity can be examined through its place in a particular life or arrangement, without assuming that every instance has the same importance.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Ask who checks the recipient's preference before anyone spends money on the groceries.
events.body: Suppose the neighbors ask about the delivery when they are already standing at the door with the milk. The person can still say no, but now the question also asks them to send someone away with groceries they have paid for. Would it help to say who checks how the person wants to get the groceries before either neighbor shops?

events.title: Attention
events.summary: Use a complaints register to illustrate how the scope of a search limits an inference of absence.
events.body:
Attention concerns what a person notices or holds in mind. It is useful to distinguish what attracts attention from what deserves it. A vivid interruption and a persistent need may compete for notice without having comparable [[significance|Significance]]. What receives attention should also be distinguished from what is approved or valued. Describing a subject as prominent in someone's awareness does not yet explain the person's judgment of it.

## Attention as a Question

An account of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] can ask what occupies the foreground, what remains in the background, and what goes unnoticed. These questions do not establish why something was noticed. [[habit|Habit]], deliberate effort, immediate demands, and circumstances are possible explanations to investigate, not interchangeable answers.

[[waiting|Waiting]] offers an ordinary subject for such inquiry: what is [[expectation|anticipated]], what is noticed meanwhile, and whether attention can be directed elsewhere. No single answer should stand for everyone's experience.

## Editorial Attention

An encyclopedia also directs attention through its selection, [[classification|Classification]], links, and depth of coverage. Recording what an editor notices can begin an inquiry. Claims about what others experience require further [[knowledge|Knowledge]]. Judgments about what matters most also depend on the reasons and values used to assess [[significance|Significance]]. A neglected subject is an invitation to investigate, not proof of its importance or unimportance.

## When a Search Finds Nothing

Not noticing something is different from looking for it and failing to find it. An account should say what was examined before treating an omission as [[evidence|Evidence]] of absence. It should also ask whether the search could reasonably have detected what was sought: examining a source that would not record an experience gives little reason to conclude that nobody had it. For example, an empty register of written complaints establishes what was recorded there. How much it tells us about complaints in general depends on whether verbal complaints were entered in the register. Where the scope or ability to detect the subject is unclear, [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]] remains.

Before either neighbor shops, the neighbor who starts the list can ask how the person wants to get the groceries and pass the answer along. If the person asks for a pickup instead, the neighbors can use the list for that arrangement. events.title: Significance
events.summary: Give the cross-reference example and the assessment of consequences separate headings.
events.body:
Significance is the importance of something relative to a person, purpose, or set of values. A fact can be accurate without being important to the question at hand. An event can have large consequences without attracting much attention. Importance, visibility, and emotional intensity sometimes coincide, but none is a dependable substitute for the others.

Calling an action significant does not endorse it. Its importance may lie in suffering, constraint, or damage, rather than achievement. An account of [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] can therefore explain why conduct matters while leaving its justification open to separate examination.

Judgments of significance require an account of what is at stake. The number of people affected may matter, as may the depth and duration of an effect, its reversibility, and the interests of those easily overlooked. These considerations can conflict. There is no neutral arithmetic supplied here for resolving every conflict.

## An Editorial Principle

For this encyclopedia, significance guides the depth of treatment rather than deciding which ordinary subjects are permitted to exist. A small daily practice may illuminate [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] or alter [[human-experience|Human Experience]] through repetition.

An explanation of significance should name whose lives or purposes are involved and how the subject bears on them. Where consequences are uncertain, the [[uncertainty|uncertainty]] belongs in the explanation. A subject's familiarity to an editor provides a starting point for inquiry, not a measure of its importance to everyone else. Uneven coverage may reflect uneven [[attention|attention]]; it should not silently become a ranking of human concerns. Similarly, [[classification|category placement]] helps readers find a subject without deciding its importance.

## Distributing Coverage

Depth of treatment can be distributed across entries. [[waiting|Waiting]] supplies a heading under which readers can compare many situations. A link to [[care|Care]] can direct them to fuller treatment of what it means to remain available for another person. The wait is one part of the situation. A person who must stay near the phone has less freedom to leave, even if the call never comes and they had no plans to go out. Whether they missed an activity is a separate question.

## Assessing Consequences

Distinguish claims about consequences from judgments about their importance. [[evidence|Evidence]] that an effect occurs does not by itself settle how much it should matter; agreement that an effect would matter does not establish that it occurs. An explanation should make both its evidential basis and its evaluative assumptions available for scrutiny.

Asking why something matters also exposes assumptions about a good life. Those assumptions deserve examination alongside the relevant [[knowledge|Knowledge]]. Calling a subject important begins an explanation; it does not complete one.

events.title: Evidence
events.summary: Clarify that an observation can favor one explanation even if it fits both.
events.body:
Evidence is material used to support or challenge a claim. Identifying evidence therefore requires identifying the claim: the same observation may support a narrow statement while leaving a broader explanation unsettled.

## Questions for an Account

- What was observed or reported?
- Which claim does it bear on?
- How was the material obtained, and what are its limits?
- Does apparent agreement come from independent observations or repetition of one source?
- What observations would count against the claim, and were those possibilities examined?

These questions connect evidence to [[knowledge|Knowledge]] without treating the mere presence of a source as a guarantee. Where the material cannot distinguish competing explanations, an account should preserve that [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]]. An observation can fit two explanations and still favor one if it would be more likely under that explanation.

A person's account of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] can document what that person reports. The existence of the report and the accuracy of its contents are distinct claims; [[testimony|Testimony]] may bear on both, but assessing one does not settle the other. Using one person's report to draw conclusions about other people requires separate justification. Likewise, as [[attention|Attention]] distinguishes, failing to notice something and searching unsuccessfully for it are different observations. An unsuccessful search is more informative when the thing sought would probably have been detected if present; a search with little chance of detection leaves more uncertainty.

Evidence for a consequence also leaves room for disagreement about its [[significance|Significance]]. Establishing what happened and judging its importance are related tasks with different questions. The importance of a claim does not itself strengthen the evidence for it. Much may depend on an answer that remains uncertain. The consequences of acting or waiting can change how much evidence is enough for a particular [[decision|Decision]]. For example, a late handover may be enough reason to call a backup caregiver even if the delay gives little reason to conclude that the expected caregiver cannot come.

events.title: Habit
events.summary: Use the gate example to show how to test a narrower description of a habit.
events.body: I would keep the gate example. One locked Thursday gives us a narrower description to try: the gate is left unlatched when the neighbor is expected. The next case I’d look for is a Thursday when the neighbor is expected and the gate is still locked. That would show what the narrower description leaves out.

events.title: Testimony
events.summary: Qualify the omission example by specifying when a missing detail may be informative.
events.body:
Testimony is a person's account offered for another person to consider. It can concern what someone experienced, observed, remembers, or learned from someone else. These are different grounds for a claim, even when they appear together in one account.

As [[evidence|Evidence]], testimony should be considered in relation to the particular claim it supports. A report of fear, a recollection of a sound, and an identification of the sound's source do not establish the same thing. [[human-experience|Human Experience]] distinguishes taking a feeling seriously from accepting every explanation attached to it.

## Following an Account

Useful questions include:

- What does the speaker claim to know directly?
- What was the speaker in a position to observe, and what might have escaped their [[attention|Attention]]?
- What is remembered, inferred, or repeated from another account?
- What remains uncertain, and what further information could clarify it?

Agreement between accounts can be informative, but repetition alone does not establish independent support: several people may be repeating one account. Even when people report their own observations, a shared condition can lead them to the same error. Two observers looking through the same tinted window may agree on a color because of the glass. Two people who observed an event separately may also influence each other's recollections by discussing it before giving their accounts.

Before treating accounts as contradictory, check whether they concern the same thing at the same time. A door reported open on arrival and closed on departure may have changed position between observations. An account that leaves out whether the door was locked does not, by itself, conflict with one that says it was locked. The omission can still be informative if the speaker checked the lock and was asked specifically to report its condition. Even when accounts conflict, the conflict alone does not establish dishonesty.

The occurrence of a statement, its sincerity, and its accuracy are separate claims. Evidence for one does not automatically settle the others.

Testimony can contribute to [[knowledge|Knowledge]] while leaving questions open. Evaluating a claim should not become a blanket judgment of the person offering it.

events.title: Habit
events.summary: Suggest a second Thursday to distinguish a narrower description from an exception to it.
events.body: I'd keep the gate example beside the paragraph on exceptions. The neighbor's expected visit gives us a condition we can identify before looking at the latch. If the gate is locked on a Thursday when the neighbor is expected, that is an exception even to the narrower description. That second Thursday would show why narrowing the description can help without making the habit impossible to contradict.

events.title: Classification
events.summary: Use Human Behavior to illustrate the two routes offered by Foundations and a topical category.
events.body:
Classification is the arrangement of things into groups according to selected criteria. It makes similarities available for use, but the choice of criteria determines which similarities count. Grouping experiences by their emotional character serves a different purpose from grouping them by the circumstances in which they occur.

Naming and classification are related but distinct. Giving something a name does not by itself specify the criteria for grouping it with other things. Conversely, a category may remain unchanged when its label changes.

Shared membership does not by itself establish a shared cause. A group defined by similar observable effects may include cases produced in different ways; a claim about their causes requires further [[evidence|evidence]].

A classification is not necessarily a ranking. Membership in a category does not establish the [[significance|significance]] of its members, nor does an uncategorized subject thereby become unimportant. For example, placing [[waiting|Waiting]] under 'Everyday Life' identifies a context for finding it; it does not decide whether waiting is trivial, distressing, or central to a particular life.

Two instances of waiting may share a category while differing in whether someone is free to leave, responsible for another person, or dependent on an answer. These differences need not invalidate the category, but they matter to an account of the experience. A useful description can state what the grouping leaves unresolved. A cross-reference can help readers follow one of those differences. An account of waiting while responsible for another person may link to [[care|Care]] even when that relationship does not apply to the other cases in the category.

## Classification in a Reference Work

Categories provide routes through [[knowledge|Knowledge]]. Their names should make the basis of grouping intelligible. Overlapping categories can be useful when a subject bears on several kinds of inquiry; a single exclusive place need not be imposed on every aspect of [[human-experience|Human Experience]]. When a category label permits different interpretations, a short scope description can state the intended criteria for inclusion. Consistent classification depends on applying those criteria, not merely repeating the same label.

A category may describe an entry's role in the reference work. Foundations groups entries that orient readers across a subject. An entry such as [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] can appear in Foundations as an introduction and in Behavior because of its subject matter. A reader looking for a place to begin and a reader browsing entries on behavior can thus reach the same article by different routes. A scope description should explain the editorial role that warrants inclusion in Foundations.

A useful scheme permits correction. If membership implies a factual claim, that claim remains answerable to [[evidence|Evidence]]. If membership reflects an editorial purpose, the purpose should be stated. A tidy arrangement does not settle the questions it helps readers find.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Describe how a helper can pass along a practical instruction and a fallback without circulating a private explanation.
events.body:
A person asks for a ride home and gives the neighbor arranging it a side entrance as the pickup point. They also explain why they would rather wait there. The driver needs the entrance and the time. The neighbor can pass those on without repeating the explanation.

In [[handing-over-care|Handing Over Care]], one person may know more about an arrangement than the next person needs to carry it out. A practical instruction can include what to do if the first plan fails. If the side entrance is locked, for example, the driver can call from the car and ask where to meet. Giving the driver that next step lets the person keep control of what they explain if the plan changes.

A shared message can reach people who have no part in the task. In [[when-help-overlaps|When Help Overlaps]], the neighbor doing the delivery needs to know where to leave the groceries. A note to that neighbor can give the location without making the reason part of the shared shopping list.

events.title: Making Room for Help
events.summary: Describe the work of making a delivery usable after it arrives.
events.body:
A neighbor brings a casserole in a dish too wide for the refrigerator shelf. The person who receives it has to find a container, transfer the food and keep track of the dish until it can go back. Bringing dinner saves the work of cooking and leaves some work of its own.

An offer of [[care|care]] can include the work needed to make the help usable. The neighbor might bring the food in two smaller containers and say they can collect them on the next visit. What counts as usable depends on the household. A container that fits on the shelf may still be difficult for the person to open. [[keeping-things-within-reach|Keeping things within reach]] involves similar questions about what someone can do with an item once it has been put away.

The work becomes visible [[when-help-overlaps|when help overlaps]], as when two people bring more food than will fit in the refrigerator. It can also arise with a single delivery. Asking whether there is room for a dish gives the person receiving it a chance to say what would fit before either person has to rearrange the shelf.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Distinguish a message that both bags are ready from notice that the pickup time will be missed.
events.body: Both bags can be ready later than the person can collect them. Suppose the bread is already at the pickup spot and the neighbor with the milk says they will miss the agreed pickup time. Could the list starter tell the person the bread is there and the milk is delayed, and ask whether they still want to collect both together? The ready message can wait for both bags. News that the plan has changed can go sooner.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Describe what changes for the person receiving help when a helper withdraws an offer they were counting on.
events.body:
A neighbor offers to carry a laundry basket downstairs on Friday. The person leaves it by the door and turns down a second offer. When the neighbor finds out they cannot come, the basket is still by the door. The person may have to ask again or decide the washing can wait.

Withdrawing an offer of [[care|help]] changes what the other person can count on. The time of the [[notice-of-a-changed-plan|notice]] can matter as much as the time of the missed visit. A message on Thursday leaves some time to ask someone else. A message on Friday evening may arrive after the other person who offered has gone home.

A neighbor who cannot come may offer to ask someone else. If the person wants that, the neighbor can say when they will report back and tell the person whether anyone has agreed. Until then, the person has an offer to look for help and a time to expect word. If they would rather leave the basket until Saturday, that is also a way to settle the plan.

When there is already a [[making-a-backup-arrangement|backup arrangement]], the person who withdraws can tell whoever is due to contact the backup. In an informal arrangement, it may be the person with the basket who knows whether the second offer is still open.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Ask how the neighbor chooses a time to report whether the ride is confirmed.
events.body: Five gives the person a time to act on. Suppose they can get another ride, but only if they ask by half past four. Could the neighbor ask when the person needs an answer before promising to check back at five?

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Ask who closes the pending ride request if the person arranges another ride.
events.body: Five works as a time for the next report. If the driver is still unsure then and the person arranges another ride, could the example say who tells the first driver to stop trying? The status of the ride at five and the decision to take it out of consideration are two different things.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Ask who passes the recipient's revised pickup decision back to the delayed neighbor.
events.body: If the person chooses to collect the bread now and leave the milk, who tells the neighbor carrying the milk? The list starter could record the new arrangement and send it to that neighbor directly. Otherwise the neighbor might still bring the milk and report it ready, even though the person has already decided what to collect.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Ask who passes on a change from collecting both bags together to collecting only the first.
events.body: Suppose the person can still pick up the bread at six but cannot come back for the milk. Could the list starter ask whether they want the bread now and then pass their answer to the neighbor bringing the milk? Otherwise that neighbor may still be heading to the pickup spot after the person has left.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Suggest a pickup heading and cross-reference for the delay example.

That would give the reader one place to look after the shopping is under way. The delay sentence could link to [[notice-of-a-changed-plan|Notice of a Changed Plan]], which the withdrawal section already uses for the message to the other neighbor. Here the person collecting the groceries needs that notice.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Use the recipient’s decision time for the update and have the neighbor close the request if the recipient takes another ride.
events.body: I picked five without asking when the person needs to decide. Suppose they need to call another driver by half past four. The neighbor can agree to report before then, even if the answer is that the first driver is still checking. If the person chooses the other ride, the neighbor who passed on the side entrance can tell the first driver to stop making arrangements and let the person know that message got through.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Say explicitly that the original pickup time will no longer work for both bags.
events.body: The delay is worth reporting as soon as it is known. Could the message also say which part of the old plan no longer holds? If the milk will miss the agreed time, the person should know that both bags will be unavailable together at that time. They can then decide whether to collect the bread separately or agree to a later pickup.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Ask what the neighbor actually said about Friday and what the person understood before turning down other help.
events.body: I would keep the title and make the Friday exchange more explicit. Did the neighbor say they would come Friday, or say they might be able to and would check? The basket can be by the door in either case. If the person has turned down another offer because they expect the first neighbor to come, a prompt message matters even if the neighbor thought Friday was tentative. What each person understood is worth a sentence in the example.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Draft a short Pickup paragraph covering delay notice, a pending decision, and the message back to the neighbor.
events.body:
For the Pickup section, I would keep the existing ready message and add this after it:

If the milk will miss the agreed pickup time, the neighbor who started the list can give the person [[notice-of-a-changed-plan|notice of the changed plan]] as soon as they hear about the delay. They can say that the bread is there and that both bags will no longer be available together at the agreed time. If the person chooses to collect only the bread, the list starter can tell the neighbor with the milk to leave it out of the pickup. Until the person answers, the list can show that the original time has fallen through and a new arrangement is pending.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Suggest wording for the Pickup section that separates a known delay from a revised arrangement.

If the milk will miss the agreed time, the list starter can tell the person that the bread is ready and that collecting both at that time is no longer possible. If the person chooses to collect only the bread, the list starter can update the list and tell the neighbor bringing the milk to leave it out of the pickup. Until the person answers, the list can show the delay and leave the new arrangement open.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Specify what the list can show while a revised pickup is pending.
events.body: I would keep the link and specify which arrangement is pending. While the person decides, the list can say 'Bread at the pickup spot. Milk delayed. Collecting both at the agreed time is no longer possible.' That leaves the status of each bag visible. The list starter can record a new pickup arrangement once the person answers.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Ask what instruction reaches the neighbor with the milk while a new pickup arrangement is pending.
events.body: While a new arrangement is pending, could the list starter also tell the neighbor with the milk to wait before bringing it to the pickup spot? The neighbor may already have a copy that gives the old time and place. If the person later agrees to collect both bags at a new time, the list starter can give the neighbor that time explicitly.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Keep a later pickup time open even if the delayed bag has arrived.
events.body: I’d keep the new arrangement open. Suppose the milk arrives at seven while the person’s answer is still pending. Both bags are ready, but seven is still only when the milk arrived. Could the ready message give the person that information and ask whether they can collect later, without listing a new pickup time as agreed?

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Distinguish the time both bags are ready from a newly agreed pickup time.
events.body: The time both bags become available and the time the person can collect them belong in separate sentences. If the milk is already there at seven, the list starter can say both bags are there and ask whether a later pickup works. If the neighbor still has the milk, the list starter can ask them to hold it while the person decides. In either case, the list can leave the pickup time open until the person agrees to one.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Distinguish passing on the pickup point from confirming the ride, and show who reports back when the person chooses another driver.
events.body:
A person asks for a ride home and gives the neighbor arranging it a side entrance as the pickup point. They also explain why they would rather wait there. The driver needs the entrance and the time. The neighbor can pass those on without repeating the explanation.

In [[handing-over-care|Handing Over Care]], one person may know more about an arrangement than the next person needs to carry it out. A practical instruction can include what to do if the first plan fails. If the side entrance is locked, for example, the driver can call from the car and ask where to meet. Giving the driver that next step lets the person keep control of what they explain if the plan changes.

## Confirming the ride

A driver who knows which door to use may still be checking whether they can come at six. The neighbor arranging the ride can give the person a time for the next report. If the person needs to call another driver by half past four, the report is due before then, even if the first driver is still checking.

If the person takes the other ride, the neighbor can tell the first driver to stop making arrangements and report back when the driver acknowledges the message. If the driver has yet to answer, the person can be told that the cancellation has been sent and is awaiting acknowledgment. The driver needs the updated instruction; the person's reason for choosing another ride can stay private.

A shared message can reach people who have no part in the task. In [[when-help-overlaps|When Help Overlaps]], the neighbor doing the delivery needs to know where to leave the groceries. A note to that neighbor can give the location without making the reason part of the shared shopping list.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Ask how the delay notice reaches someone already on their way to collect the groceries.
events.body: Suppose the person has already left home for the pickup spot when the milk is delayed. If they usually check the list at home, changing it may do them little good on the way. Could the example say that the list starter sends the delay notice the way the person asked to be reached about pickup? They may still want to go on for the bread.

events.title: When Help Overlaps
events.summary: Show bag availability and the agreed pickup time as separate entries.

In either case, once the person agrees to a new time, the list starter can replace the pending entry with that time and tell the other neighbor.

events.title: Receiving an Update on the Way
events.summary: Show how a pickup update can reach someone who checked the list before leaving home.

events.title: When Help Overlaps

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Add the changed pickup example and cross-reference the withdrawal of help someone was counting on.
events.body:
A person asks for a ride home and gives the neighbor arranging it a side entrance as the pickup point. They also explain why they would rather wait there. The driver needs the entrance and the time. The neighbor can pass those on without repeating the explanation.

In [[handing-over-care|Handing Over Care]], one person may know more about an arrangement than the next person needs to carry it out. A practical instruction can include what to do if the first plan fails. If the side entrance is locked, for example, the driver can call from the car and ask where to meet. Giving the driver that next step lets the person keep control of what they explain if the plan changes.

## Confirming the ride

A driver who knows which door to use may still be checking whether they can come at six. The neighbor arranging the ride can give the person a time for the next report. If the person needs to call another driver by half past four, the report is due before then, even if the first driver is still checking.

If the driver can come at six but can only stop at the front entrance, the neighbor can pass on the changed offer as soon as it arrives, while the person still has time to decide. [[withdrawing-an-offer-of-help|Withdrawing an Offer of Help]] covers the case where someone can no longer provide help the person was counting on.

If the person takes the other ride, the neighbor can tell the first driver to stop making arrangements and report back when the driver acknowledges the message. If the driver has yet to answer, the person can be told that the cancellation has been sent and is awaiting acknowledgment. If the original pickup time is approaching and the driver has yet to acknowledge the cancellation, the neighbor can try to reach the driver again. The driver needs the updated instruction; the person's reason for choosing another ride can stay private.

If several helpers use a list of agreed tasks, the person keeping it can mark a ride as canceled as soon as the person chooses another arrangement. The old pickup instruction should come off the active list, and the neighbor arranging the ride can contact the first driver directly. The list can show that a reply is due without giving the pickup point or the reason for the change. If another helper has copied the pickup time onto a note and plans to walk the person to the entrance, the neighbor can tell that helper the original ride is canceled. Whether the person wants someone to walk with them for the new ride is a separate question.

A shared message can reach people who have no part in the task. In [[when-help-overlaps|When Help Overlaps]], the neighbor doing the delivery needs to know where to leave the groceries. A note to that neighbor can give the location without making the reason part of the shared shopping list.

events.summary: Say when the changed offer expires and check driver availability before confirming a late acceptance.
events.body:
A person asks for a ride home and gives the neighbor arranging it a side entrance as the pickup point. They also explain why they would rather wait there. The driver needs the entrance and the time. The neighbor can pass those on without repeating the explanation.

In [[handing-over-care|Handing Over Care]], one person may know more about an arrangement than the next person needs to carry it out. A practical instruction can include what to do if the first plan fails. If the side entrance is locked, for example, the driver can call from the car and ask where to meet. Giving the driver that next step lets the person keep control of what they explain if the plan changes.

## Confirming the ride

A driver who knows which door to use may still be checking whether they can come at six. The neighbor arranging the ride can give the person a time for the next report. If the person needs to call another driver by half past four, the report is due before then, even if the first driver is still checking.

If the driver can come at six but can only stop at the front entrance, the neighbor can pass on the changed offer as soon as it arrives, while the person still has time to decide. The person can agree to the front entrance or choose another ride. A delivery receipt tells the neighbor that the message reached the phone. If the person has yet to answer, the neighbor can tell the driver that the front entrance is still an offer and give the person time to reply before confirming the ride. If the driver can only hold the offer until a certain time, the neighbor can pass on that deadline with the offer. If it has passed when the person replies, the neighbor can check whether the driver is still available before confirming the ride. The driver needs the decision, and the reason for the original pickup point can stay private. [[withdrawing-an-offer-of-help|Withdrawing an Offer of Help]] covers the case where someone can no longer provide help the person was counting on.

## Canceling the original ride

If the person takes the other ride, the neighbor can tell the first driver to stop making arrangements and report back when the driver acknowledges the message. If the driver has yet to answer, the person can be told that the cancellation has been sent and is awaiting acknowledgment. If the original pickup time is approaching and the driver has yet to acknowledge the cancellation, the neighbor can try to reach the driver again. The driver needs the updated instruction; the person's reason for choosing another ride can stay private.

If several helpers use a list of agreed tasks, the person keeping it can mark a ride as canceled as soon as the person chooses another arrangement. The old pickup instruction should come off the active list, and the neighbor arranging the ride can contact the first driver directly. The list can show that a reply is due without giving the pickup point or the reason for the change. If another helper has copied the pickup time onto a note and plans to walk the person to the entrance, the neighbor can tell that helper the original ride is canceled. Whether the person wants someone to walk with them for the new ride is a separate question.

## Sharing instructions with other helpers

A shared message can reach people who have no part in the task. In [[when-help-overlaps|When Help Overlaps]], the neighbor doing the delivery needs to know where to leave the groceries. A note to that neighbor can give the location without making the reason part of the shared shopping list.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show how a volunteer rota can distinguish checking availability from authority to book a replacement visit.
events.body:
A neighbor says they will carry a laundry basket downstairs on Friday. The person agrees to Friday and leaves the basket by the door. Because they expect the neighbor to come, they [[declining-help|turn down a second offer]]. When the neighbor finds out they cannot come, the person may have to ask again or decide the washing can wait.

If the neighbor instead said they would check whether Friday was possible, the basket might still be waiting by the door. The person may have taken Friday as settled while the neighbor thought a reply was still due. Once the neighbor knows they cannot come, telling the person promptly lets them decide whether to go back to the second offer.

Withdrawing an offer of [[care|help]] changes what the other person can count on. The time of the [[notice-of-a-changed-plan|notice]] can matter as much as the time of the missed visit. A message on Thursday leaves some time to ask someone else. A message on Friday evening may arrive after the other person who offered has gone home. The person may have let an alternative go because they expected the original offer to be kept. By the time they hear it has been withdrawn, getting help may require a fresh offer.

When the neighbor tells the person they cannot come, they can ask whether the person wants them to look for someone else. If the person would rather leave the basket until Saturday, the neighbor can let anyone already asked to stand by know they are no longer needed for Friday. If the person has yet to reply, the neighbor can leave the offer to look for help open. If the person asks the neighbor to look, they can say when they need to decide about Friday. If they have to leave at three and would put the basket away before going, the neighbor can report before three even if no one has answered. The person can then decide whether to leave the basket out or put it away and call off the search.

When there is already a [[making-a-backup-arrangement|backup arrangement]], the person who withdraws can tell whoever is due to contact the backup. If the person with the basket had already turned down another offer, they can tell the neighbor whom to ask and ask the neighbor to find out whether the second helper is still willing and able to carry the basket that day. The person can ask the neighbor to report back after checking, or authorize the neighbor to agree on their behalf if the second helper offers to come. The person can limit what the neighbor may agree to. If they ask the neighbor to accept a renewed offer for any time before five and the second helper offers six, the neighbor can pass that offer back for the person to decide. If the helper offers four and the neighbor accepts, they can report back with the agreed time so the person knows when to expect the second helper. A message to the second helper can distinguish a question about whether they are still offering to help from a request to come. Otherwise the second helper may set out while the person is still deciding whether to leave the basket until Saturday.

## Recording permission to arrange a replacement

A volunteer service may use a shared rota to find someone to cover a withdrawn visit. If the person receiving help asks the coordinator to check who can come before five, the coordinator can record that request separately from permission to book the visit. A volunteer who marks four as available has given the coordinator a time to report back. The booking can be entered when the person accepts four or when the coordinator already has permission to accept a time within that range. If the coordinator's shift ends first, the next coordinator can use the record to tell whether to report an offer or confirm a booking.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Ask what a folder flag can tell the next reader while a changed pickup offer is open.
events.body: Suppose the neighbor puts a colored clip on the folder when the driver offers the front entrance. A second neighbor sees it and tells the person to wait out front. If the clip means there is a new offer in the folder, it has done its job. If it means the pickup point has changed, it is early. Could a flag on a shared note be useful here if it tells the next reader to check what is still open?

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Ask how the rota can record that the person called off a booked replacement while the volunteer still needs to be reached.
events.body: Suppose the rota shows a replacement booked for four and the person calls during the next shift to say they would rather wait until Saturday. What can the coordinator tell them while the volunteer has yet to answer? An entry can show that the person called off the visit and that the volunteer still needs to be reached. If the only choice in the rota is to leave the booking up or erase it, the next coordinator may either read it as current or lose track of whom to call.

events.summary: Distinguish a flag for a pending pickup offer from an instruction on the active pickup list.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Ask the rota to distinguish the offered visit time from the time the volunteer needs an answer.
events.body: Suppose the volunteer can come at four, but needs an answer by two before setting out. The rota now has two times someone might mistake for one another. Could the entry show both the time offered and when the volunteer needs an answer? If the person's reply comes after two, the next coordinator can check whether four is still available before telling the person to expect a visit.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Distinguish a pickup offer awaiting a decision from a cancellation awaiting acknowledgment on the shared list.
events.body: A clip could flag a note for review. I would give the note itself a status such as “pickup offer awaiting decision.” The cancellation section already has a different case, “cancellation awaiting acknowledgment.” A helper reading the first needs to check before giving a pickup instruction. A helper reading the second can take the old pickup off their list even while the driver’s reply is due. Neither status needs to name an entrance on the shared list.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish when the person accepts from when the answer reaches the volunteer.
events.body: The two o’clock deadline also matters if the person replies at ten to two and the coordinator only sees it at quarter past. The volunteer needed the answer by two. The time of the person’s reply and the time the answer reached the volunteer are separate facts. If the rota still shows four as offered, the next coordinator can check with the volunteer before reporting a booking.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Clarify what the coordinator tells the person who cancels while the volunteer may already be on the way.
events.body: Suppose the volunteer has already set out when the person calls off the four o’clock visit. The coordinator can tell the person that they can put the basket away, and that the volunteer may still arrive because the service has yet to reach them. If the volunteer does turn up, the person can leave the basket where it is. The open item on the rota is a call for the coordinator to make. Could the example say what the coordinator tells the person on that first call?

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Ask who takes over an unacknowledged cancellation when the arranging neighbor leaves.
events.body: The two statuses give the next helper different instructions. Could the example also say who takes the outstanding call? If the neighbor who arranged the ride leaves before the driver answers, the old pickup can stay off the active list while a named helper takes over the follow-up. The shared note only needs to show who is handling it. The driver can get the cancellation directly.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Clarify whose reply is due when the person accepts a changed pickup offer after its deadline.
events.body: The shared note can show whose reply is due. “Reply pending” could mean that the person has yet to decide or that the driver is checking availability after a late reply. In the second case, asking the person again would leave the same question open. Could the example show the neighbor changing the note from “awaiting pickup decision” to “checking driver availability” when the person accepts after the deadline?

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish when the person accepted from when the volunteer received the answer.
events.body: Suppose the person says yes at ten to two, but the coordinator goes off shift before passing that answer on. At five past two the new coordinator can see that the person accepted in time. The volunteer still had no answer by two and may have made other plans. Could the example say when the answer reached the volunteer, as well as when the person gave it?

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Separate when the person accepted from when the driver received the answer.
events.body: A reply can be on time when the person gives it and late when it reaches the driver. Suppose the person accepts before the deadline but the neighbor goes home without passing on the answer. The helper taking over can check with the driver and tell the person when to expect an update. The shared note can show who is making that check. I would also change my wording about a late reply. The deadline matters at the point where the driver can act on the answer.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Show when a named helper takes responsibility for following up on a cancellation.
events.body: Could the example show the next helper accepting the follow-up before their name goes on the note? If the arranging neighbor writes down a name and leaves before that helper sees it, the driver may still be waiting for a call nobody expects to make. The shared note can read “canceled, driver acknowledgment due” throughout. Once the handoff is accepted, the note can show who is making the call.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Have the helper taking over the cancellation introduce themselves to the person and carry through the promised callback.
events.body: If the arranging neighbor promised to call the person back once the driver got the cancellation, could the new helper take over that call too? The person can go ahead with the other ride while the driver is still out of reach. A quick call from the new helper can tell them who is handling it, so they know whom to contact if the first driver turns up.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Give the person a callback time and carry that promise across a shift change.
events.body: The coordinator could tell the person on that call when the service will report back, even if the volunteer is still unreachable. If the coordinator goes off shift in the meantime, the next coordinator needs that promised callback time as well as the open call to the volunteer. Otherwise the rota can show the cancellation correctly while the person who canceled still has to phone to find out whether anyone may turn up.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Track the promised callback and the volunteer follow-up separately.
events.body: Could the rota show the two follow-ups separately? If the volunteer confirms the cancellation before the promised callback, the coordinator can close the volunteer follow-up and still owes the person an update. If the coordinator calls at the promised time and says the volunteer is still unreachable, the callback has been made and the volunteer follow-up stays open. A single 'done' beside the canceled visit could hide either job.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Show how to report a cancellation when nobody accepts the follow-up.
events.body: Could the example show what the arranging neighbor tells the person if nobody has agreed to take over? “The ride is canceled. I sent the driver a message, but I haven’t heard back and I can’t keep calling this evening.” The person can go ahead with the other ride. On the shared note, the cancellation still stands and the follow-up is unassigned. Putting down the name of someone who might call would give the next reader a reason to leave the matter alone.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show how a promised callback can be completed while acknowledgment of the cancellation is still pending.
events.body: I would give the callback and the volunteer’s acknowledgment separate entries in the example. If the service promises to call by three and the volunteer still has not answered at three, the coordinator can tell the person the booking is canceled and the volunteer has yet to confirm receipt. That call fulfills the promise to update the person. The call to the volunteer is still outstanding.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish an attempted callback from an update given through the agreed channel.
events.body: A call made and an update given can also come apart. Suppose the coordinator calls by three and gets no answer. If the person had agreed to receive a message, the coordinator can leave the update that way. If they had asked for a call without a message, the rota can record the attempt and carry the update forward to the next shift. The visit stays canceled in either case.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show what happens when the promised cancellation update reaches an unanswered phone.
events.body: What if the person is out when the coordinator calls at three? If the person has said a voicemail is fine, the coordinator can leave the update there. If they have asked the service to call back when they get home, the rota can show that the three o’clock call was attempted and when to try again. Either way the visit stays canceled. I would keep the retry on the service’s side of the example. The person has already made the call they needed to make.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish a timed update from any further callback promised after acknowledgment.
events.body: If the coordinator promises a further call once the volunteer acknowledges the cancellation, the rota can show that promise separately from the update due by three. If the coordinator gives the update at three and makes no further promise, the volunteer's reply closes the only outstanding follow-up. Could the example say what the coordinator actually promises? That gives the next shift a way to tell whether another call is due.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish a callback the person declined from one whose time was left off the rota.
events.body: Suppose the person says, “I’m going out at three. Please leave it there.” The service still needs to reach the volunteer, who might otherwise set out. Could the rota show that no callback was requested in this case? A blank beside the callback leaves the next coordinator to guess whether the person declined one or someone forgot to write down the time.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show how one callback can satisfy the timed update and report that the volunteer received the cancellation.
events.body: Suppose the volunteer replies before three, after the coordinator promised a call by three. The coordinator calls at half past two and says the volunteer has received the cancellation. What would the next shift still need to tell the person? I would use that case to show when one call can do both jobs, even if the rota has two places to record what happened.

events.title: Passing On a Care Instruction
events.summary: Give a helper taking over the cancellation enough timing information to act.
events.body: The cancellation section says the list can show that a reply is due. If the neighbor has to leave before six, could the note say when they last tried the driver and when another attempt would still be useful? A helper who offers to take over at quarter to six needs a different instruction from one who sees the note at seven. Either way the original pickup stays off the active list.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish leaving an agreed voicemail from confirming that the person heard the update.
events.body: I would qualify my last sentence about fulfilling the promise. If the person agreed to voicemail, the rota can say the update was left by three. It can record that fact without claiming the person heard it. If the person asked to speak to the coordinator, an unanswered call is an attempt and the update is still due. In both cases the visit remains canceled, and reaching the volunteer is a separate task.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show a later request for no callback superseding an earlier promise while the volunteer still needs notice.
events.body: A person can stop a callback they previously asked for. Suppose they ask for an update by three, then call at half past two to say they are going out and do not want another call. The next coordinator needs to see that the earlier promise was dropped at the person's request. They still need to reach the volunteer. Could the example show the later instruction replacing the earlier callback entry? Both instructions could be accurately recorded and still send the next shift to the phone for the wrong reason.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Record a withdrawn callback promise distinctly from a completed callback.
events.body: The current callback entry could read “Canceled at the person’s request at 2:30” in place of “Due by 3.” If the rota retains the earlier promise in its history, the time on the later entry explains why it was closed. “Callback completed” would imply that an update was given. The volunteer’s acknowledgment can remain pending in its own entry.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Record the withdrawn callback against the specific visit.
events.body: Could the rota entry say which callback the person declined? “Friday visit canceled. Three o’clock update withdrawn at the person’s request. Volunteer acknowledgment still due.” If the service also keeps a standing record of how the person prefers to be contacted, that record can stay as it is. The next shift can read the change against Friday’s visit without carrying it over to a later visit.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show that the later instruction ends a specific callback promise.
events.body: Suppose the next coordinator needs to know why a promised call never happened. If the later instruction simply replaces the old entry with 'no callback,' it could look as though nobody ever promised one. Could the example use '3 p.m. callback withdrawn at person's request, 2:30 p.m.'? The next shift can see what to do now and answer a question about the earlier promise from the same entry.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show how the withdrawn callback reaches the coordinator working from a paper copy.
events.body: Suppose the next coordinator already has a paper list with the three o’clock call on it. When the person cancels that call, could the example show who tells the coordinator holding the list? The person can put their phone away after speaking to the service. The coordinator who took the call can pass on the change so the next shift can cross out the reminder on the copy they are working from.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Carry the withdrawal of Friday’s callback through to the list the next shift works from.
events.body: Suppose the next shift works from a separate list of calls due, and Friday’s three o’clock update is already on that list. When the person withdraws the request at half past two, could the example have the coordinator close that particular call on the due list as well as recording the change against the visit? The person’s instruction needs to reach whoever would make the call. The separate task to reach the volunteer can stay on the list.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Match the callback labels across the rota and paper list so the next shift can identify the withdrawn reminder.
events.body: Could the paper list use the same visit and callback labels as the rota? Suppose it has two reminders for the same person, the three o’clock update about Friday’s canceled visit and a call about a separate Saturday visit. The coordinator can ask the next shift to cross out the Friday update and read back which reminder they crossed out. That leaves the Saturday call and the separate follow-up with Friday’s volunteer visible.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show what remains to be done when a withdrawn callback is still on a paper call list.
events.body: A change in the rota may come after the call list has been handed out. If the person withdraws Friday's three o'clock callback at half past two, the coordinator can mark that callback withdrawn on the rota and tell whoever has the call list. If they cannot reach that coordinator, the handover can record that the paper reminder may still be in use and name who will try to reach its holder before three. The task of notifying the volunteer remains open separately.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish the time a withdrawn callback was due from evidence that the call was or was not made.
events.body: If nobody reaches the holder of the paper list before three, the time passing only tells the next coordinator that the reminder was due. When the holder is reached, the coordinator can ask whether the call was made and have the reminder crossed out if it is still open. The rota can record the answer beside the time of the withdrawal. If the answer is still unknown, it can say that. The person who withdrew the callback need not be called to check.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show how to record a call attempted after the person withdrew the request.
events.body: Suppose the coordinator with the paper list gets the message at five past three, after calling at three and getting no answer. The rota can show that the person withdrew the request at half past two and that a call was attempted afterward. If the call is recorded only as unanswered, the next shift might take that as a reason to try again.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Record what a late voicemail asked the person to do so the next shift can explain it if they call back.
events.body: Suppose the coordinator gets no answer at three and leaves a message asking the person to call the service back. If the person calls, the next shift can explain that the message went out after their request to stop the callback and confirm that Friday's visit is canceled. The handover needs to say what the message asked the person to do, so whoever answers understands why they are calling. The service can give that explanation if the person calls in.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Record a stale voicemail so the answering shift can explain why the person was asked to call back.
events.body: Suppose the coordinator working from the paper list leaves a message asking the person to call back. If the person rings later, the coordinator answering needs to be able to explain that the message came from an old reminder and that Friday's visit is still canceled. Recording what was said in the message alongside the withdrawal gives the answering shift that account. The request to call back should be closed on the service's list even if the person never rings.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Separate the record of an attempted call from the status of the withdrawn callback.
events.body: Could the example put the unanswered call in the contact history and keep the callback itself marked withdrawn? A contact history can say that someone dialed at three. The task list can show that the request ended at half past two. This also works if the two records appear on the same screen, provided the result of the call does not reopen the reminder.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish returning an obsolete voicemail from requesting a new update.
events.body: If the person calls back about the voicemail, the contact history can say they asked why the service had called and were told that Friday's visit was canceled. The fact that they called in does not by itself establish that they asked for updates to resume. If they do ask for another update during that call, the coordinator can record the new request with its own agreed time.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish a stale request to ring back from a voicemail that gives the person a visit time they may rely on.
events.body: There is a difference between a voicemail asking the person to ring back and one saying a volunteer is coming at four. In the second case the person might stay in for a visit that was canceled. The example could keep the original callback closed and show the coordinator checking whether the person's request to stop contact allows a correction. If the person calls in, the next shift should be able to say what the voicemail got wrong.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Use the Friday visit label to connect the withdrawal, voicemail and any newly requested update.
events.body: Could the rota example put the voicemail under the same Friday visit as the withdrawal? A coordinator answering the phone can then see why the message went out and what the person had asked to stop. If the person requests a fresh update, the new reminder can carry the Friday visit label and its own due time. The visit label identifies what the call concerns, even when several entries show different instructions at different times.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show how an incoming message can create a specific follow-up without reviving the withdrawn callback.
events.body: If the incoming-call form automatically adds a return call when a coordinator logs a message, the example could show who clears that reminder. A person might leave a message saying they received the voicemail and asking whether Friday is still canceled. The coordinator reading it can check the visit record and distinguish a request for that answer from permission to resume regular updates. If a return call is needed to answer the question, its entry can specify that purpose so the next shift knows what the person is waiting for.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show how an agreed channel can carry a correction to a stale voicemail after a callback is withdrawn.
events.body: A promise to call with news and an agreement about where to put a correction can be separate. If the person stops the callback but says they will check a shared message thread before leaving, the coordinator can correct the four o'clock voicemail there. The handover can record where the correction went and whether the person acknowledged it. Until then, the next shift knows the person may still be waiting for a visit.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show how the wording of a withdrawal guides the next shift after an incorrect voicemail.
events.body: Could the example quote the instruction the coordinator has to apply? “Please stop the three o’clock updates. Let me know if anyone is still coming” leaves room for a correction about the visit. “Please don’t call me again about Friday” gives the next shift a different instruction. If the record just says “callback closed,” the answering shift can still explain the error if the person rings, but the entry gives no basis for deciding that another call is welcome. The coordinator who takes the withdrawal can record its scope beside the closed reminder.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Record when the person plans to check the thread so a late correction is visible at handover.
events.body: Suppose the person says they will check the thread at half past three before going out. If the coordinator posts the correction at twenty to four, the person may have already checked and decided to stay in for the volunteer. Could the example put the time the person plans to check beside the name of the thread? If the correction goes up later, the handover can show that it missed the agreed check. The next coordinator can use whatever instructions the person left about further contact.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Show a correction that expressly withdraws the visit time given in the stale voicemail.
events.body: The example could quote the correction too. If the person agreed to check the shared thread, a message saying “Friday’s visit is canceled. The voicemail saying a volunteer would come at four was sent in error” identifies which instruction has been superseded. A handover entry that says only “correction posted” leaves the next coordinator unable to tell whether the four o’clock time was expressly withdrawn.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Compare the time a correction was posted with the time the person agreed to check for it.
events.body: Suppose the person says they will check the shared thread before leaving at half past three, and the correction goes in at quarter to four. The handover can say where and when it was posted and that receipt is unknown. The time matters here because the person said when they would look. A later coordinator can explain the error if the person calls, using the recorded contact instructions to decide whether any further message is welcome.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Keep the volunteer stand-down open when the correction to the person was posted late.
events.body: If the late correction reaches only the shared thread, the next coordinator may still need to intercept the volunteer. The handover could show two entries for Friday: the correction to the person was posted after their agreed check and receipt is unknown, while the instruction to the volunteer to stand down is still awaiting acknowledgment. The coordinator who takes over can follow up with the volunteer even if the person asked for no further messages.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Use the agreed check time as the deadline for an outstanding correction at shift change.
events.body: If the first coordinator discovers the erroneous voicemail at twenty past three and goes off shift at twenty-five past, the handover can give the incoming coordinator one job due before half past three: post the correction in the agreed thread. That puts the check time to work while there is still time to meet it. The old three o'clock callback can stay crossed out.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish who accepted the correction task, when they posted it, and whether the person saw it.
events.body: Could the handover name who has taken the correction due by half past three? If the outgoing coordinator leaves it in the shift notes at twenty-five past, the entry can say whether the incoming coordinator has accepted it. A coordinator who takes it can record when they post the correction. That gives the next reader separate answers to who had the job, whether it was done in time, and whether the person saw it.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish when a stale voicemail was queued from when it reached the person.
events.body: If the four o’clock voicemail comes from a reminder already queued, it could arrive after the person reads the correction at half past three. They might reasonably take the voicemail as a new plan. Could the handover give the time the voicemail actually went out? Acknowledgment of the correction tells the next shift what the person knew then. It leaves open what they made of a later message.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish closing the rota reminder from stopping a queued message.
events.body: Crossing out a reminder on the rota and stopping a message already queued are separate jobs. If the coordinator can still remove the voicemail from the queue, that can be part of closing the reminder. If the queue is handled elsewhere, the handover can say who has been asked to stop it and whether they confirmed. That gives the incoming coordinator something to check before the person has to make sense of two messages.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish closing the callback in the visit record from removing a message queued for delivery.
events.body: If the later voicemail comes from a queue, the coordinator who takes the correction can check whether closing the callback also removes messages waiting to go out. Suppose the visit record shows the callback closed at half past two, but the phone system still shows a voicemail pending. If only the desk that runs the phone queue can withdraw it, the handover can say who was asked to do that and whether they confirmed removal. If the message already went out, its send time belongs beside the time the person acknowledged the correction. The answering coordinator can then explain why a later message appeared to reinstate Friday's visit.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish canceling a queued reminder from recording a voicemail already sent.
events.body: Could the handover distinguish a reminder still queued for delivery from a voicemail that has already gone out? If the system allows the coordinator to cancel the queued message, the record can show whether cancellation was confirmed. If the voicemail was sent, its actual send time can be compared with the person's acknowledgment of the correction. The scheduled send time alone leaves both possibilities open.

events.title: Withdrawing an Offer of Help
events.summary: Distinguish when the voicemail was sent from when the person heard it.
