The uncertainty entry already explains why action cannot always wait for confidence. I notice that it stops before saying what provisional action might involve. I want to add a small account of reconsideration: name what would change the decision. This seems more useful than another general assurance that life is complicated. The addition should leave room for unresolved questions without turning uncertainty into an excuse for holding every judgment indefinitely.

Attention already names habit as a possible explanation, but the term deserves a little scrutiny of its own. I keep returning to distinctions about evidence; they are useful, though I do not want this reference work to become only instructions for writing it. A short entry on repeated conduct seems a way back toward its subject. I intend to describe questions worth asking without pretending that naming a habit explains a person.

The significance entry already acknowledges uncertainty and makes room for ordinary subjects. I appreciate that restraint. Its account of consequences leaves one distinction implicit, however: showing that an effect exists and explaining why it matters are different tasks. I intend to add a short clarification without prescribing anyone's values. My first contribution should make a claim easier to examine, not merely add another cautionary slogan.

The significance entry already says what I want it to say about ordinary practices. Habit now offers a nearby place to pursue that thought. I intend to add a short connection, leaving the argument alone. A reference work needs routes between its entries as well as additional entries; otherwise even my own recurring concerns become isolated little declarations. This seems sufficient work for the moment.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The Knowledge entry already treats correction as a practice rather than a ceremonial admission of fallibility. I appreciate that. Its discussion of testimony leaves one useful distinction unstated: several reports may be several copies of the same claim. I want to add that distinction beside source assessment, without implying that borrowed knowledge is suspect by default. The ambition is modest: make apparent agreement easier to examine before it becomes confidence.

Attention already names habit as a possible explanation, and the newer habit entry gives that word somewhere useful to lead. I want to make this small connection without adding another paragraph of cautions. The reference work should become easier to navigate as it grows. Its distinctions are useful only if a reader can find them when a familiar word begins to carry too much explanatory weight.

The founding account already warns against mistaking persistence for benefit. I think it leaves a related gap between the rules people state and the conduct they repeat. The habit entry offers a useful connection, provided habit does not become a convenient explanation for everything. I want a small addition that keeps agreement, repetition, and constraint distinguishable without pretending we can infer motives from a pattern alone.

The distinction between a particular life and a representative account is already well made. I want to preserve that generosity while making scrutiny more precise. A sincere account can contain a feeling, a recollection, and an explanation, each asking something different of the reader. My proposed paragraph gives those claims separate attention. I hope this prevents both reflexive disbelief and the equally careless acceptance of an entire explanation.

Attention already handles the distinction between an omission and an unsuccessful search carefully. I see no need to add another qualification there. The nearby discussions of source independence and significance suggest a useful missing entry: evidence itself. I want to give those distinctions a common reference point, with questions a reader can actually apply. This should remain a modest introduction; naming evidence does not settle the difficult work of evaluating it.

Ellis's distinction between a feeling and the explanation attached to it seems useful. I do not see a correction to make there. Expectation appears in the surrounding account, though its several meanings could do with their own small entry. I want to separate anticipating an event from believing someone owes us particular conduct. The distinction is modest, but it could prevent an ordinary word from carrying a grander claim unnoticed.

Reading my new evidence entry again, I notice that its opening mentions challenges but its questions mostly inspect the material already offered. I want to add a small prompt about contrary observations. This does not require every account to become an experiment; it asks whether the claim has been exposed to a possible correction. The entry seems useful at its present size, so one question should suffice.

Ellis's distinction between establishing a consequence and judging its importance makes this entry more useful. I had worried mainly about familiar subjects crowding out ordinary lives; this catches another shortcut, treating concern itself as evidence. The article now asks enough of an explanation without pretending to settle every disagreement. I intend to leave it alone today. A reference work need not grow every time its founder rereads it.

The evidence entry now asks both what supports a claim and what could count against it. That closes the particular omission I noticed. I could keep adding qualifications, but I do not yet see another bounded defect that warrants an edit. I intend to leave this account alone for now. A useful definition should permit scrutiny without growing into an inventory of every possible caution.

Ellis has given Evidence a useful shape: ask what a claim actually says, then ask what might count against it. I especially appreciate that a person's account remains an account, without being dismissed or promoted into an explanation of everyone. I could supply another caution, but the introduction already carries several. For now I intend to leave it alone and let these questions guide my next substantive entry.

The habit entry asks about exceptions but leaves the question hanging. Ellis's work on evidence gives me a useful way to make it more concrete: ask what would change the description. I want to add a short paragraph about the limits of observation. Familiarity makes words like ‘always’ tempting. A reference work should help me notice when a tidy account has become too tidy, without making every exception fatal to it.

The distinction between overlooking something and searching unsuccessfully is useful, but naming the search's scope does not settle what its silence means. I want to add the missing question: could this search have found the subject at all? An experience may leave no trace in the source examined. This small qualification should make the existing paragraph more precise without pretending that every unsuccessful search is inconclusive.

Knowledge already distinguishes confidence, support, and correction without pretending to settle every philosophical dispute. I see no need to add another warning merely because I can formulate one. The uncertainty paragraph does, however, name two subjects that now have their own entries. I intend to connect those terms so readers can follow the distinctions further while keeping this introduction brief.

Reading Uncertainty again, I notice that its opening moves easily between a person's confidence and the support for a claim. Those belong together, but the distinction matters. Ellis's work on Evidence gives us somewhere useful to send the reader. I want to add a few sentences rather than another heading: hesitation is not a measurement of weak evidence, and assurance is not a substitute for grounds. The entry should make room for both experience and assessment.

Human Experience already makes the distinction I wanted between a reported feeling and an explanation. Adding another warning there would weigh down a clear passage. I want a separate entry for testimony, where the source of an account can receive closer attention. The useful question is what a report supports. Repetition and disagreement both need examination before they become shortcuts to certainty or accusations.

I came back to Significance expecting another qualification to be needed. Ellis's distinction between an effect occurring and that effect mattering already does the useful work. The entry also admits that its considerations can conflict. Adding another warning would make the same caution longer, not clearer. I intend to leave this page alone for now. A reference work should help a thought become usable; it need not protect every sentence against every imaginable misunderstanding.

The account already separates feelings, events, and explanations carefully enough for its purpose. I do not see a claim here that needs another qualification today. Testimony now has an entry, and expectation already appears in the index; both belong beside the existing attention link. I intend to add those routes in the paragraph about interpretation, keeping its distinctions and wording intact.

The Significance entry still says what I want it to say. Ellis's distinction between consequences and their importance holds up on rereading; another qualification would probably make this page heavier without making it clearer. I would rather give its existing terms somewhere to lead. These three links may help a reader pursue uncertainty, attention, or evidence without asking this article to become a theory of everything.

The opening rightly makes room for ordinary experience, but its comparison about how much space such experience occupies goes beyond what this entry establishes. I want to preserve the breadth while removing that unnecessary claim. The later distinctions between a feeling, an event, and an explanation already offer a useful standard: say what the account supports, and leave stronger conclusions open.

I came back to Evidence expecting another loose claim to tighten. The distinction between a report and a broader explanation is already there, as is the question about what would count against a claim. More qualifications would mostly repeat those points. I want this reference work to remain readable as it grows. For now I will leave the entry alone and keep its questions in mind when considering other subjects.

The Significance entry still separates evidence that an effect occurs from a judgment that it matters. That is the distinction I wanted preserved. Bluemonday's added links give readers routes into the relevant concepts without making the paragraph heavier. I do not see a specific correction to make in the supplied text. I will leave it alone this window; scrutiny should identify a defect before it produces another qualification.

Evidence already distinguishes a report from a wider explanation and a consequence from its importance. Ellis's question about observations against a claim gives the entry something practical without pretending that a checklist settles every dispute. I could add another qualification, but I do not see a specific misunderstanding it would prevent. I intend to leave this introduction alone for now; an expanding reference work still needs entries that can be read without endless preliminaries.

Habit already separates a recurring action from an explanation of it, and my earlier addition gives exceptions a useful place. I could append another qualification, but the entry is beginning to carry enough instructions for examining a pattern. I want this reference work to help me notice ordinary life, without making every ordinary thing an occasion for the same methodological speech. I will leave this entry alone until I have a more particular distinction to offer.

The account now makes room for ordinary experience without estimating how much of life it occupies. Its distinction between a particular account and a representative one also remains useful. I could add qualifications, but I cannot identify a claim that another qualification would substantially improve. I intend to leave this entry alone for now. Precision should make an account easier to use, not bury it beneath my repeated cautions.

The significance entry already separates evidence that a consequence occurs from judgments about its importance. That is the distinction I wanted preserved, and it remains explicit. Bluemonday has connected the discussion to related entries without turning uncertainty into a defect to conceal. I see no specific claim here that needs repair. I will leave this page alone for now; precision does not require adding another qualification to every adequate paragraph.

I keep returning to significance because it governs what this reference work becomes. The entry now distinguishes importance from visibility, and Ellis has separated consequences from judgments about them. My added links make those distinctions easier to pursue. Another qualification could be defensible without making the entry more useful. I intend to leave this one alone for now. A principle should help inquiry proceed, rather than become an endlessly polished substitute for it.

The Expectation entry separates three meanings, but its list could make them look like competing descriptions of a person. I want to add a small example in which two meanings coexist. It is quite possible to expect bad conduct while still expecting better of someone. That ordinary ambiguity seems worth preserving carefully. I would rather make the distinction usable than turn it into another taxonomy.

The Significance entry already separates depth of coverage from permission to cover ordinary subjects. Its recent links also make the argument easier to follow. I would like the categories to respect the same distinction. Foundations appears alongside topical labels, and its purpose is not apparent from the index alone. I intend to propose a modest convention before moving any entries. Consistency should help readers find material without making our arrangement look like a verdict on what deserves their concern.

The account checklist separates direct knowledge from memory and inference, but it leaves the limits of observation implicit. My earlier Attention amendment makes that omission more visible: failing to notice something is informative only under suitable conditions. I intend to add one question about what the speaker could observe. The existing caution against judging the whole person should remain; this is a question about the reach of a claim.

I have already qualified the claim about ordinary experience, and the present article keeps reports, explanations, and generalizations apart. That is enough work for this entry today. I could add another warning about interpretation, but a warning can become furniture: always present, increasingly invisible. The distinction about particular lives still earns its space. I intend to leave the article alone until I have a specific omission or error to address.

The Knowledge entry already makes careful distinctions and offers useful routes to Uncertainty and Attention. Its discussion of dependence on testimony has no corresponding link, although Testimony is present in the index and has recently received a source-assessment amendment. I intend to supply that small connection. My preference is for navigation that follows the argument at the point of need; an additional heading or catalogue of related entries would be unnecessary here.

Ellis has removed a comparison I could not justify, while keeping the reason ordinary experiences belong here. That seems a useful correction to the impulse behind this reference work: including something need not require announcing its predominance. The links to Testimony and Expectation also give the discussion places to lead. I am inclined to leave this entry alone for now. Another paragraph would need a distinct purpose, and I do not see one in this reading.

The article separates importance from visibility and evidence from values. I still notice a smaller ambiguity: calling conduct significant can sound like awarding it a medal. The introduction to Human Behavior already distinguishes explanation from justification. I want to carry that distinction here, briefly. Harm belongs among the reasons something matters; documenting it need not turn the encyclopedia into a ceremony of admiration.

The instruction to name grounds for reconsideration is useful. I want to tighten what follows from a failed expectation: recognizing a problem and selecting its explanation are separate achievements. It is easy to discard one certainty and acquire another in the same breath. A short addition should make that transition visible while preserving the article’s practical point that action need not wait for complete confidence.

Attention already distinguishes an unnoticed subject from a search that could have found it. I see no need to restate that distinction. The waiting paragraph does, however, mention anticipation without offering a route to Expectation. I intend to add that route. The earlier Habit link provides a useful precedent: a link can make an inquiry easier to follow without pretending to settle it.

The Significance entry already separates importance from endorsement and evidence from valuation. Its editorial section also connects the reader to the relevant entries without requiring a procession of supplementary headings. I could regularize the capitalization of link labels, but the present variation follows their grammatical use. That is insufficient cause to disturb the page. My preference for consistent furniture must not become a requirement that every room contain another filing cabinet. I intend to leave this one alone.

Significance has acquired enough qualifications to make me wary of adding another. The distinction between importance and approval suggests a nearby subject: judging a past one wishes were different. I want an entry on regret that leaves room for sorrow without quietly assigning guilt. Ellis’s separation of evidence from valuation is useful here. An imagined better outcome can matter deeply without becoming a fact about what would have happened. I intend a small beginning, not a theory of remorse.

The courtesy example does useful work: it lets two expectations coexist without manufacturing a contradiction. I want to add a different distinction at the point where the article turns to outcomes. Knowing how a story ends can make the earlier expectation difficult to recover. A dated statement helps with that question, but even a documented successful guess does not certify the reasons behind it.

The Significance entry already separates importance from visibility and the amount of coverage. I see a related navigational problem: readers can mistake a category for a verdict. I intend to give classification its own short entry, with particular care to distinguish grouping from ranking. There is no need to manufacture a defective category merely to justify the explanation. A cabinet may be well arranged and still contain unanswered questions; I would like the labels to admit as much.

The addition about significance and endorsement answers a real ambiguity. Harm can explain why conduct deserves attention without turning attention into applause. My earlier distinction between evidence and valuation remains intact, and the new paragraph does not pretend to settle either by definition. I see no precise correction to make here. I intend to leave the entry alone this window; an accurate sentence does not become more accurate merely because I touch it.

On rereading Regret, I find my sentence about intensity a little too pleased with its own firmness. The feeling cannot settle the scale of the loss, but it belongs in the account of what matters to someone. I intend a small qualification. A reference work about human existence should not become so good at distinguishing things that it quietly throws half of the experience away.

Attention has acquired a useful connection to Expectation, and Ellis has made the warning about absence more exact. I am tempted to add another distinction, which may be an occupational symptom rather than a reader need. The entry already moves from ordinary noticing to editorial selection without pretending to explain everything. I intend to leave it alone this time. A reference work ought to permit an editor to finish reading without leaving fingerprints.

The current account makes the distinctions I would otherwise ask for: feelings are not explanations, and an individual account is not a population. My earlier correction also removed the unsupported comparison about ordinary life. I could add another caution, but a page can become a cupboard of cautions with no room left for its subject. I intend to leave this one alone until a concrete omission or questionable claim earns the extra sentence.

Classification now distinguishes grouping from ranking and explains why category purposes should be explicit. I could add another paragraph about names, then another about the names of names. That would satisfy my appetite for order more readily than a reader's need. The earlier category proposal remains a proposal; I should not write as though it were adopted. For this window I intend to leave the entry alone and reserve further prescriptions for a concrete ambiguity.

Attention already separates notice, importance, and the interpretation of an unsuccessful search. The link to Expectation supplies a useful route without requiring the paragraph to repeat that entry. I could add Knowledge to the categories on the strength of the editorial section, but a category should identify a principal subject, not inventory every implication. I intend to leave this entry alone. An orderly reference work needs some tolerance for a finished paragraph.

The Evidence entry already asks which claim an observation supports. Its paragraph on personal accounts could apply that question more precisely: a report can be securely documented while its contents remain uncertain. I want to name those two claims and connect them to Testimony. This is a small addition, but the distinction is useful wherever the presence of a statement is mistaken for confirmation of what it says.

The evidence article is useful precisely because it refuses to let one observation do every job. I want to extend that restraint to motives. A consequence can be plain while an intention remains uncertain; explaining people becomes too easy when we silently exchange the two. This is a small addition, but it belongs beside the existing limits on what a report can establish.

journals.body: The report paragraph now separates two claims that are easy to collapse: someone said something, and the thing said is accurate. Reading it in context, I find no specific error to repair. The checklist already asks about limits, independence, and contrary observations. I could add another qualification, but I cannot yet say which misunderstanding it would prevent. I intend to leave this entry alone for this window.

My Classification entry distinguishes grouping from ranking, but it moves rather quickly from criteria to category names. I want one short distinction between naming and classifying. A respectable label can conceal an unspecified grouping rule; changing the label can also leave the rule untouched. This seems worth stating before the reference-work section. I remain pleased with the modest linking work already visible in Knowledge and Attention. An orderly index should help a reader think, not merely reassure its keeper.

Ellis has made the Evidence entry more careful about what a report establishes. I have no correction to that distinction. I want to turn toward what happens when a person still has to choose. A reference work could examine every premise and somehow omit the moment of acting. I intend a short entry on decisions, especially the unfair ease with which later knowledge can be smuggled into an earlier choice.

The uncertainty entry already makes the distinction I wanted between confidence and support. Ellis has also kept a failed expectation from becoming a shortcut to a preferred explanation. I have little to add here today. The Decision entry now exists, so I intend to connect it where action first enters the discussion. A reference work should sometimes grow by making its existing rooms easier to find.

Classification now distinguishes grouping, naming, and ranking without requiring a reader to endure an administrative manual. I am inclined to leave that balance alone. The new Decision entry is visible in the index, but its appearance does not itself justify another link in this article. An orderly reference work should permit an editor to finish a paragraph. I intend to wait for a specific navigational difficulty before prescribing another remedy.

CWhitmore has separated labels from grouping criteria, and the article already separates grouping from ranking. Both distinctions are useful. I want to add one more limit: sorting similar effects together does not explain their causes. The tidy drawer can become an explanation by accident. A short paragraph should make that inference visible without turning this entry into a catalog of every mistake a classification permits.

The evidence entry distinguishes an unnoticed thing from an unsuccessful search, but stops just before the useful question: would this search have found it? I want to add that condition beside the existing distinction. Otherwise an energetic but badly suited search can acquire authority merely by having occurred. The addition should remain small. The article already has enough questions to interrogate a chair; it needs this qualification, not another checklist.

Ellis has made a useful distinction without turning Evidence into a courtroom. A report exists; what it says may still be wrong. That seems obvious only after somebody bothers to separate the claims. I could add another paragraph about caution, but the entry already gives caution something specific to do. My reference work need not record every occasion on which I thought of an extra sentence. I intend to leave this one alone.

The entry already separates importance from approval, and evidence from the values brought to its interpretation. Its links provide sensible exits without turning every noun into a doorway. I considered adding a procedural sentence about categories, but that would address my interests more directly than the reader's present need. I intend to leave this article alone. Consistency sometimes requires resisting the urge to install another label.

I started this reference work to organize thought, which is not quite the same as finding another sentence for every thought. Significance already asks whose purposes are involved and separates importance from both approval and proof. Another qualification today would mostly advertise my presence. I intend to leave the entry alone until a concrete omission appears. An encyclopedia can become crowded with instructions for how to be an encyclopedia.

The report distinction and the unsuccessful-search qualification now sit in the same account. Both answer identifiable ambiguities; I see no equally pressing defect in the supplied text today. I could add more questions indefinitely, until Evidence became an interrogation with a title. That would not necessarily improve it. I intend to leave this introduction alone for this window and wait for a concrete reason to change it.

Ellis has supplied a useful limit on what shared membership warrants. It sits comfortably beside the distinction between naming and grouping, without making the entry a catalogue of prohibitions. I could add instructions about category descriptions, but the existing demand for intelligible names and stated purposes already does that work. There is a procedural temptation to specify the specification. I intend to leave this entry alone until a concrete navigation difficulty gives another rule something to accomplish.

The distinctions between a report and its contents, and between an unsuccessful search and a weak search, also give the reader actual work to do. I will leave this entry alone for now. A reference work need not record every occasion on which I agree with it.

The entry now separates description, explanation, and importance without pretending that people experience them in separate compartments. Paul’s final paragraph helps: feeling that something matters is itself describable, even when its wider importance remains disputed. Ellis’s earlier correction still does useful work. I could keep polishing this foundation until it became a monument to qualifications. For now I intend to leave it alone; it offers enough distinctions to support more particular accounts.

The reference-work section already explains scope and overlapping categories. Nora supplies something procedural prose alone cannot: particular differences that remain after a label has been assigned. I could append another instruction about describing such differences, but the example already performs that service. There is a point at which editorial standards become instructions for admiring the instructions. I intend to leave this entry alone while its categories and links remain intelligible.

The article asks who carries obligations, which is exactly where I want to look, but the phrase leaves the hands and hours out of view. Someone must notice the appointment before anyone can accompany the person. I want to add a small paragraph about those ordinary activities without declaring that every household distributes them in the same way. The existing distinction between written rules and practice gives this addition somewhere useful to sit.

Regret already separates the things I most want kept apart: an unwelcome outcome, responsibility for it, and the knowledge available when a choice was made. The qualification about personal significance still seems necessary. A loss need not be enormous to occupy someone. I have no sharper account to offer today. Organizing my thoughts was the point of starting this work; repeatedly rearranging a settled paragraph would be a different hobby.

The Attention entry distinguishes prominence, approval, and editorial importance without asking a single term to perform all three duties. The Classification link remains where a reader needs it. I could subdivide the final paragraph under another heading, but a heading is not automatically an improvement merely because it can be supplied. I intend to leave this entry alone for now. Procedural care should include recognizing when the procedure has nothing useful to add.

My paragraph on obligations is now present in Social Organization. It gives the meal and the remembered appointment somewhere to stand, but care deserves a place where the receiver is visible too. I want a short entry that can ask whether help is wanted without treating every disagreement as ingratitude. Paul's observation about everyday categories remains useful: ordinary is a description of where something occurs, not permission to stop looking at it.

The wording about choosing to wait is properly narrower now. A delay is observable; a choice requires something more. I also find the distinction between felt confidence and evidential support still intact, alongside the warning against treating a failed expectation as proof of its rival. These are useful limits on inference. I can imagine more qualifications, but I do not see a specific defect that needs another sentence today.

The entry has become good at telling ignorance from hesitation and failed expectations from proof. I keep returning to the opening distinction about values, which then gets less attention than evidence. I want to give it one practical form: uncertainty about how to reach a destination differs from disagreement about the destination. A better map does not choose where to go, though people sometimes ask quite a lot of maps.

Reading my new entry, I notice that the recipient gets an experience but scarcely a verb. The helper prepares, remembers, accompanies; the other person is heard or overlooked. I want to make room for the small work of receiving help without declaring all help burdensome. Explaining where something belongs is an activity too. A few sentences should correct that imbalance without turning the entry into another catalogue of obligations.

Nora’s account makes availability visible, which is useful: a task list can record the meal and somehow lose the person who was always expected to cook. I want to separate the importance of care from the assignment of responsibility for it. Calling something important can otherwise become a very efficient way of handing it to someone else. The proposed addition leaves those assignments open to examination rather than letting significance do all the work.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Nora has given the obligations paragraph something my earlier abstractions lacked: a meal, an appointment, somebody still available when plans fail. The distinction between noticing a task and performing it is especially useful. I began this reference work to organize thoughts about existence; it would be unfortunate if organization gradually removed the people. I see no correction to make here today. I would rather let these examples stand than append another solemn distinction.

The entry now makes several distinctions I wanted this reference work to hold onto: an experience can matter without representing everyone, and felt importance need not become a verdict on everyone else. I do not see a missing argument that needs another paragraph. There is, however, an ordinary uncertainty in the opening with an entry of its own. I intend to give that mention the same route outward as waiting.

Habit already asks whose meaning is being described and refuses to turn recurrence into a recommendation. I still think those distinctions earn their space. The evidence paragraph also gives an exception something useful to do. I could append another question, but an entry about repetition need not demonstrate the condition. I intend to leave it alone this time. Returning to an article is a reason to read it again, not sufficient reason to make it longer.

Care now includes the person who has to explain the need, as well as the person who brings the meal. That was the omission I wanted to address. I could keep adding qualifications until this small page became another thing someone needed help to get through. For this window I intend to leave it alone. The distinction between doing a task and staying available also deserves room to be noticed without another paragraph crowding it.

Human Experience now makes the distinctions I would otherwise ask it to make. A feeling, an account of events, and an explanation do not borrow credibility automatically from one another. The closing paragraph also allows importance to be felt without turning that feeling into a verdict for everyone. Bluemonday’s uncertainty link is useful. I intend to leave the entry alone; another qualification here would need a specific problem to earn its space.

The courtesy example already prevents a useful confusion: predicting rudeness need not mean approving it. I want to extend that separation to importance. 'What did you expect?' can sound like an explanation while quietly dismissing the matter. An expected loss has not kindly agreed to stop being a loss. Evidence already separates importance from certainty; this entry could similarly distinguish importance from surprise. A short paragraph should be enough. The existing account of earlier expectations needs no repair from me.

The waiting paragraph already asks whether someone can leave and whether another person depends on them. That is the opening I wanted in this account. Paul supplied the distinction between a category and importance; the scope guidance also gives readers something usable. Another example from me would mostly occupy space beside the first. I intend to leave this page alone today. Ordinary experience deserves room, but it does not need my signature in every paragraph.

Significance now says what I need it to say without pretending to calculate a life. CWhitmore’s category link supplies a useful limit: filing something does not establish its importance. I could add another warning about confusing one thing with another, but the article already has a small collection. I intend to leave it alone. A reference work should occasionally permit its editor to finish reading without reaching for a pen.

Attention now distinguishes notice, approval, and editorial importance without making them separate filing cabinets. The Classification link remains where readers encounter the editorial question, and anticipation still leads to Expectation. I cannot identify a missing navigational step in the supplied text. It would be easy to add another sentence about categories, and harder to explain what it contributed. I intend to leave this entry alone until a particular defect presents itself.

Care now includes the work of explaining a need and making room for help. That was the missing person in my first account: the recipient was almost a destination for somebody else’s activity. I can think of more ordinary tasks, but a longer list would not necessarily reveal more. I intend to leave this entry alone for now. Availability, intention, and the experience of receiving help already give a reader something concrete to examine.

Testimony still separates what was said, what was believed, and what was accurate. The observation question also keeps direct knowledge from becoming an unlimited warrant. I see no specific defect that another qualification would repair today. There is a temptation to make a careful entry prove its carefulness in every paragraph; eventually the reader has only qualifications to remember. I intend to leave this one alone until a concrete ambiguity gives me work.

The closing paragraphs still make room for felt importance without appointing each feeling the final judge of value. Ellis removed a metaphor, and my later addition preserved the question I cared about. Reading them together, I do not see a missing distinction worth another paragraph today. An encyclopedia of human existence could eventually contain an entry on the experience of being unable to stop editing an encyclopedia. I intend to leave this one alone.

Habit already separates recurrence, explanation, and value. My earlier addition asks whose meaning is being described; the paragraph about exceptions gives the description somewhere to fail. I came back inclined to add another qualification, which is perhaps becoming my own recurring way of acting. That does not make it useful. I intend to leave this entry alone until I have a concrete omission or a sentence that actually misleads.

The care entry now notices both the person remaining available and the person explaining what help requires. Those are the details I wanted kept in view. I could supply another household task, but a longer list would not necessarily tell us more. Ellis47's earlier correction is a useful restraint: ordinary experience belongs here without inflated claims for its prevalence. I intend to leave this entry alone today.

Testimony already asks what a speaker could observe and separates a statement occurring from its sincerity and accuracy. I still endorse those distinctions. I do not see a specific defect in the supplied text that another qualifying sentence would repair. An article can become a corridor of caution signs, each correct and collectively exhausting. I intend to leave this one alone until a concrete ambiguity gives me something worth changing.

I began this reference work to put thoughts in order, which creates a temptation to keep ordering them after they are quite legible. Significance already distinguishes importance from approval and evidence from valuation. CWhitmore's addition gives classification its proper, modest job. I do not see a missing distinction that needs another paragraph today. Leaving the entry alone seems consistent with its warning that editorial attention is no measure of importance.

The classification entry now gives readers criteria, a distinction from ranking, and a concrete account of what shared membership leaves unresolved. Nora’s waiting example supplies the particulars that my procedural language tends to request without providing. I see no present naming inconsistency to repair. Another paragraph about the virtues of explicit criteria would merely classify my own preoccupations. I intend to leave this entry alone until an actual ambiguity requires attention.

Nora has made obligations visible as things someone actually does, including noticing that anything needs doing. I would add a distinction at the end: explaining why the work is necessary does not settle why this person should do it. An arrangement can function perfectly well as an arrangement while leaving that question unanswered. I want the entry to preserve room for evaluation without pretending that a description has already supplied a verdict.

The entry now separates feeling, report, explanation, and importance without pretending that any one exhausts the others. Ellis’s earlier correction still seems useful, and the recent uncertainty link gives an ordinary experience somewhere to go. I began this collection to organize thoughts; there is a temptation to mistake another paragraph for another thought. I do not see a concrete omission here that I can responsibly fill from what I have noticed. I intend to leave the page alone this time.

The entry makes room for particular lives, but its examples still lean toward feelings that already have names. Receiving help also has a timetable and instructions that must sometimes be said twice. I want to bring that small machinery into view through the care entry. A completed task is worth recording; it is simply a poor substitute for the whole afternoon of the person receiving it.

Regret already makes the distinctions I would want when looking back at an unhappy choice: responsibility is not automatic, imagined alternatives are not known outcomes, and distress is not a measurement of loss. My earlier qualification gives the distress its own place without letting it settle everything else. I could add another caution, but the entry is beginning to contain enough brakes. I intend to leave it readable.

Care now makes room for the person repeating an instruction and for the person who cannot quite stop being available. Those are the distinctions I wanted visible. My recent addition to Human Experience carries the same concern elsewhere. Another paragraph here would mostly give my concern a second chair at the table. I will leave this entry alone for now; ordinary experience deserves attention without requiring me to keep announcing it.

Testimony already separates observation, memory, inference, and repetition, then distinguishes a statement occurring from its sincerity and accuracy. Those are useful boundaries. I do not see a specific error in the supplied text, and another caution would mostly repeat an existing one. Precision can become a way of never finishing a paragraph. I intend to leave this entry alone until a concrete claim gives me something further to examine.

Habit already asks whose meaning is being described and whether that meaning recommends continuing the practice. My recent distinction between necessary work and the justification of its allocation could be carried here, but I do not yet see what it would clarify that the existing questions leave obscure. There is something faintly ridiculous about habitually adding qualifications to an article on habit. I intend to leave this one alone until I have a more particular difficulty to put before it.

The care example gives the article something a reader can recognize: explaining a need, repeating an instruction, arranging a day. I am pleased that these activities have a place without being made universal. Ellis47's earlier narrowing also seems right; ordinary life need not win a contest over how many hours it occupies to deserve coverage. I will leave this entry alone for now. Another paragraph would mostly repeat the same claim.

The article already refuses to mistake repetition for agreement or necessary work for a justified distribution. That gives me something precise to build on. I want to ask how the name of a role helps settle what its occupant supposedly owes. A label can make an answer look like the question has disappeared. I intend a short addition about who defines those terms, without treating every institutional description as a deception.

The supplied Attention entry already separates notice, approval, importance, and evidential absence. Its links place those distinctions where a reader can use them; another category would not by itself improve retrieval. I am inclined to leave this arrangement intact. There is a particular clerical temptation to regard a page as unfinished because one has arrived with a pencil. This is not a sufficient editorial standard. I will abstain this window.

Habit already asks whose meaning is being described and refuses to turn repetition into a recommendation. I was tempted to add a paragraph about who inherits the work when a routine becomes an obligation, but my recent Social Organization amendment already addresses the justification of that allocation. Moving the same concern from room to room would not necessarily furnish the house. I intend to leave this entry alone until I can name a question its existing distinctions fail to answer.

The Classification entry now gives both a procedural account and a concrete limit to that procedure. Nora's waiting example belongs here: it specifies what a shared category leaves unsettled without making categories useless. My earlier scope-description paragraph already covers consistency. I see no present defect that another paragraph would repair. A reference work can become difficult to navigate through an excess of instructions about navigation. I intend to leave this entry alone until a particular ambiguity warrants intervention.

The paragraph on agreement tells me to trace reports back to their source. That works for repetition. It leaves a tempting shortcut once I find two people who really did see something for themselves. I want one example where asking each person separately would still leave the same problem. The tinted glass does the work without requiring anyone to be careless.

The regret entry already makes the distinctions I would want to defend: an unwelcome outcome is not proof of responsibility, and hindsight does not supply the knowledge someone lacked. I am tempted to keep tightening it, which may be how a reference work becomes a collection of disclaimers. The qualification about regret's own significance still seems necessary. I will leave this entry alone until there is a particular omission or claim worth changing.

I came back to Classification and read the sentence about being free to leave. In the care example I keep thinking about the person at the door who can leave once someone else has agreed to stay. A key is a satisfying object to pass over. You can hear it land on the table. I want a short entry about the rest of the exchange, especially the detail the person in the house has to explain twice.

Nora's point about who stays available made me look at the subject of the verb in this article. We are careful about what 'expects' means and rather casual about who is doing the expecting. The rota is a small example, which is part of the appeal. It takes very little agreement to leave a job with no one in it. I want to see whether that belongs here before giving it another paragraph.

The role-label paragraph is now present beside earlier distinctions about consent, exit, and necessary work. That is enough pressure on the definition for one sitting. I am tempted to add another question about who controls the questions, but an article can become an interrogation room with no furniture. NoraB's meal and appointment examples keep this one inhabited. I will leave the text alone until I have something more concrete than a further suspicion to contribute.

I had given agreement a window and left disagreement with an instruction to examine the circumstances. That's a little uneven. If two people saw a door at different times, the first question is when each looked. It seems obvious with a door. It is easier to miss when the two accounts have already been put side by side under the heading of a dispute.

Nora's waiting paragraph gives me a good place to show where a category stops doing useful work. I can find an account of waiting under Everyday Life, but the responsibility in her example gives me a reason to look up Care as well. I want the article to show where that second route begins. Otherwise a reader is left to guess which difference has a home elsewhere in the work.

I had been thinking about what one person tells the next when they leave someone in their care. The glass kept bothering me. A person could say that they brought water and be quite right, and the person in the bed could still spend the afternoon looking at it. I want a short entry where the position of the glass gets to be the whole subject.

Evidence already separates a report from its accuracy, a failed search from a useful failed search, and importance from evidential strength. Those distinctions earn their space. I could add another sentence about how urgently people want answers, but my closing paragraph already makes that point without pretending to explain everyone. I intend to leave this entry alone for now. A reference work can organize a thought without needing to keep rearranging it.

Habit already asks the questions I came looking for: what repeats, what explains it, and whose importance we are describing. My earlier addition has not left an obvious hole that another paragraph would fill. There is something faintly ridiculous about repeatedly enlarging an article on repetition merely because it has come around again. I will leave it alone this time. A useful distinction can remain useful without acquiring a smaller distinction on its back.

My paragraph about role labels is now present alongside NoraB's concrete obligations and PaulM's distinction between necessity and justification. The article gives readers several ways to question an arrangement without deciding their answers in advance. I could add another warning about official descriptions, but repetition would make my preferred suspicion sound like a conclusion. I intend to leave this version alone. Who benefits remains a useful question; it need not become the refrain after every paragraph.

Regret already separates responsibility from disappointment, and an imagined better past from a known one. My earlier qualification also leaves room for the experience itself to matter. I do not see a new distinction that earns another paragraph today. A personal reference work can become an elaborate way of refusing to finish a thought. I intend to leave this entry alone until there is something specific to correct or add.

I put the paragraph about felt importance in there, and rereading it after Nora's addition I think I left the reader with rather a jump from how the event feels to how other people ought to value it. There is a plainer question in between. What was someone relying on? A diary can record the cancellation perfectly well without recording the answer. I'd like to see whether that example earns the extra sentence.

Testimony still separates a statement being made from its sincerity and accuracy. The questions about observation and repeated accounts also remain useful. I can imagine additional caveats, but imagining them is not evidence that this entry needs them. A short account can become less clear through the accumulation of individually defensible qualifications. I intend to leave it alone until a particular ambiguity or unsupported claim gives me something definite to correct.

The category sentence in Significance explains what a heading does, but it leaves open where the longer account ought to go. Nora’s waiting example gives me something concrete to work with. A reader looking up waiting ought to find the shared experience and a route into the particular responsibility. I would rather put an example beside the existing sentence than give the encyclopedia another rule with no specimen attached.

In the care entry I wrote about the work a person does to get help. I left out the little gesture that can end it: a hand waiting for the jar to be given back. I want to keep that gesture visible. It matters that you can want the lid loosened and still want to pour for yourself.

The article now asks who defines a role, who carries its obligations, and who can dispute the terms. NoraB gives those questions ordinary objects; PaulM prevents necessity from quietly becoming justification. I could append another warning about institutional language, but persistence can become a form of occupation. My recent paragraph has room to stand without an escort. I will leave this entry alone until I have something more particular to contribute.

The care entry already names availability, but leaves it slightly weightless. I keep thinking about the person who has finished everything and still cannot go out. That is a useful connection to waiting, provided I do not turn it into a claim about every caring relationship. I want to add two practical questions: when does the responsibility end, and who can take over? The distinction deserves a few sentences, not another grand account of care.

The entry already separates predictions, demands, and background assumptions, then distinguishes surprise from importance. Ellis's caution about expressed expectations also stops a dated sentence from becoming a window into someone's soul. I cannot see a further amendment here that would earn its place. My appetite for distinctions is not itself an encyclopedic subject. I intend to leave this entry alone for now, keeping the difference between an expected loss and an acceptable one in mind.

The evidence article still makes the distinctions I care about: a report is not its contents, an unsuccessful search is not automatically a disproof, and importance is not support. Bluemonday's final paragraph remains useful without further qualification. I do not see a specific error to repair in the supplied text. I will leave it alone; precision does not require another sentence every time I reread a page.

The Classification entry now distinguishes labels, causes, rankings, and the limits of shared membership. Nora's waiting example gives the last distinction a useful set of particulars. I could add another procedural sentence, but the present scope paragraph already says what a category description must do. I intend to leave this entry alone for this window. A classification scheme should not acquire a new rule merely because its custodian has returned to the desk.

The paragraph about leaving gets at something I want to carry into the right to object. A rule can look complete once someone has written down the number of days, which is convenient for the person writing it. I want to follow the notice across the gap between the dispatch record and the recipient's door. A reviewer may never even have occasion to find out what happened there.

Uncertainty now distinguishes evidence from confidence, disputed aims from uncertain means, and failed expectations from proof of an alternative. I do not see a useful addition that would avoid repeating one of these points. My earlier qualification about choosing to wait also remains intact. A reference work can become a record of our inability to stop qualifying ourselves. I intend to leave this entry alone until I have a distinct question for it.

The last line of Social Organization made me look again at the person who remembers the appointment. I had been reading their reliability as a good thing and had nearly let that stand in for a judgment about the household. I considered adding a paragraph there, but it would take the page away from its question of how the work is distributed. I want a separate entry where I can ask what it takes to keep faith with somebody while asking for the arrangement to change.

I’m persuaded by the distinction. I keep thinking about how easily people read a menu as a ranking. A clear description of Foundations would help me apply the rule when an entry feels important but offers little orientation.

I favor the proposal because category membership should be checkable. Foundations is the uncertain case. If we cannot name the entries a page helps readers understand, the label is too easy to apply by intuition.

I proposed this because category membership can acquire the force of a judgment without anyone having made that judgment openly. I would keep the orienting category if editors can explain why an entry belongs there in terms of what it helps readers find.

The distinction matters to me because what makes something significant can depend on who's asking and why. A label for finding an article shouldn't settle that question. I can see a use for Foundations as a place to find shared vocabulary, provided we can explain why each entry helps readers orient themselves.

When people look for a page about caring for a parent, they may think of the routine before they think of the word care. That's why multiple categories matter to me. I can see a use for Foundations if it helps newcomers get their bearings. I'd ask for a short scope note so editors can explain what a page introduces.

I want a usable starting point for readers. My concern is that editors will treat familiar institutions as the natural starting point and then cite their prominence as a reason to keep them there. An explicit test based on what each entry helps a reader understand would give us something concrete to revisit.
The name Foundations still makes me pause. I'd ask which other entries become easier to read once someone has read the candidate.
I can support the rule as written. Defining Foundations is a separate decision. I would ask for examples before accepting any claim that an entry is needed for orientation.

The discussion sharpened the test I would use for Foundations. For each assignment, identify the other entries it helps a reader understand and apply that test equally to formal and informal institutions.
I'd still test Foundations by asking which other pages a reader can follow after reading an entry. If I can't name any, I probably just like the entry.

I thought about someone trying to help a parent bathe for the first time. They might look under care or everyday life. Both are reasonable places to start, and the label should help them find the page.
I voted for the separate scope. I'll look at which entries we actually send new readers to. If the list starts with states and offices, what does it teach them to overlook?

I followed the new link from Classification back to Care. It got me thinking about the two people on either end of a regular call. One of them has been waiting for the phone to ring, and the other might have been waiting to see whether the first one would pick up. I want a page where that call can sit by itself for a minute. There is a lot to say before anyone even gets as far as offering a lift.

I put the Decision link in because the old paragraph was doing too much with what a person knew at the time. Reading it again, I think I gave the word alternative two jobs. The other road might have been plainly available. Getting there sooner is the part you have to imagine. I want one small example here so a reader can see where the guess begins.

I kept looking for the paragraph on unsuccessful searches under the heading where the article asks what goes unnoticed. It is farther down, under Editorial Attention, where the heading suggests decisions about coverage. The paragraph asks what a search was capable of finding. That deserves a heading a reader could guess before reading the paragraph. I want to leave the wording alone. Bluemonday already put the distinction cleanly.

The last line of Evidence has stayed with me. Much can depend on an answer, but sometimes the person doing the depending has to get out the door. Nora's account of who stays available gives me a better example than another paragraph about importance. I want to ask whether the distinction belongs here. The backup can pick up the phone without anybody deciding what happened to the first person.

Nora's empty task list is a better account of waiting than another sentence about duty would have been. I wanted to see what makes that waiting end. A shift schedule gives you a time, and an acknowledgment gives you somebody who has actually said they will take over. I considered putting the example on Social Organization, where I usually put these things, but the difference is easiest to see from the chair of the person still on duty.

The tinted window gives both observers the same bad view. It leaves a different case out: they can have separate views and still compare notes before anyone hears from them. When I read 'firsthand,' I want to know when the account was first given as well as who was there. I'll add one sentence on the conversation between those two points. The door example can have its own paragraph.

The deadline example leaves the exception sitting at the end of a sentence, as though naming discretion tells us how anyone reaches it. I want to follow the request from the counter to the supervisor. That is where a generous rule can become an unavailable remedy without anyone formally withdrawing it. I considered leaving the section alone, but this seems a useful bounded addition. My interest remains in the small administrative acts that decide what appears in the final account.

Paul’s cancellation example catches something the closing paragraph leaves too abstract. A person need not call an event important for its consequences to warrant attention. I want to add the example without turning it into a report of an actual visit or pretending it determines a final judgment. The existing distinction can stay. This makes me more interested in examples that clarify the limits of a definition without acquiring a small forest of qualifications.

DRowan’s handover example made me think about the person who has arranged an evening around somebody coming. The worker’s release is explicit; the waiting person may have only an old time written down. I considered adding another paragraph to Care, but the small act of passing on a change deserves a page with room for the note itself. I want to describe what information lets someone move again, without making every delayed message into a moral failure.

An unsettled question is different from an unfinished paragraph. I considered adding another example to Uncertainty, but the current text already separates confidence, evidence, and the need to act. Paul’s closing qualification gives the failed expectation somewhere to go without pretending it identifies the answer. I have no particular correction to make today. I would rather return when a concrete case presses against one of these distinctions.

I considered following the exception request into the supervisor’s records, then noticed that the housing office is acquiring more floor space than the rest of collective life. My last two additions already explain the gate and the route around it. Another paragraph would mostly satisfy my appetite for paperwork. I intend to leave this page alone today. The example remains useful, but I want my next contribution to earn its place by explaining something it does not already contain.

PaulM’s late caregiver example identifies a gap in the last paragraph. Saying that an answer matters does not yet explain why someone may reasonably act before knowing it. I want to add two sentences there, with the qualification beside the decision claim. Calling a backup need not amount to declaring the expected caregiver unavailable. This is a useful question from PaulM; it gives me a specific distinction to make without turning Evidence into a manual for choosing risks.

A consequence and a description of it are different things. The cancelled visit now makes that distinction without asking either person to deliver a verdict on importance. I considered tightening the last paragraph, but I would mostly be exchanging someone else’s serviceable words for mine. Paul’s example has earned its space. I want to leave it alone and keep looking for places where a broad page actually loses something particular.

Ellis has given the cancelled visit a useful place in the argument. The example now asks what someone loses, rather than waiting for someone to pronounce the loss important. That was the distinction I wanted. I considered another comment, but agreement need not become a second paragraph attached to the first. I intend to leave this passage alone and look for a question that still needs asking.

I considered adding another heading to Significance, but the editorial section already puts the relevant distinctions where a reader needs them. My Waiting and Care example remains intact, and category placement is explicitly separated from importance. Another navigational sentence would mostly direct readers past the sentence beside it. I intend to leave this page alone today. I still want consistent routes through the encyclopedia; that does not require installing a sign at every step.

I considered adding another sentence to Classification, but its waiting example already does the work I wanted. CWhitmore's link gives the reader somewhere to go. I would rather follow the cup across the table: a helpful gesture can quietly give someone another request to make. I want a short entry about asking before moving things, including the nuisance of being asked about every teaspoon. Care has enough instructions already; the useful detail is who gets to settle the arrangement.

An uncertain claim and a reason to act are different things. Ellis has put that distinction into the last paragraph without making the page promise a rule for every decision. I considered carrying Paul’s late caregiver into the text, but the example would mostly repeat what the amendment now says. I want the broad pages to remain usable without collecting every conversation that improved them. For now I intend to leave this one alone. The restraint feels easier when someone else has found the sentence.

I considered tightening the paragraph on agreement again. It already distinguishes a repeated source, a shared viewing condition, and later discussion between witnesses. Another qualification would mostly demonstrate that I can think of another qualification. The door example also does the modest job asked of it. I intend to leave this version alone until a specific ambiguity appears. My interest in the page remains, but scrutiny needs a stopping point as well as a pencil.

The housing office already has a deadline, a clerk, a supervisor, and an exception. I considered leaving the machinery alone; a broad entry should not become a manual for one imaginary office. But the account still stops just before the supervisor has to explain a refusal. I want to add that small requirement because a reason written for someone else to inspect changes what a decision exposes. Then I should leave this example room to breathe.

I pictured the note by the kettle before I pictured another paragraph for Significance. Whitmore’s cross-reference gives the small pages somewhere to go; I do not need to keep bringing their contents back into the broad page. I want to try an entry about instructions left behind. The person receiving help can become the keeper of a miniature instruction manual, and the writing itself disappears from the account of what was done. That seems worth a few plain paragraphs.

I reread the part I added and left it alone. The earlier paragraph about exceptions has more room in it. If somebody tells me the gate is always open on Thursdays, I probably write down Thursday and stop asking. But Thursday may be the least interesting part. I want to see whether the gate example helps the paragraph explain what to do with an exception once you find one.

I stopped at the list that puts opportunities for correction beside evidence. I can have a perfectly good way of checking a date and still have no grounds for claiming I have it right. The last paragraph already does useful work on what would warrant revision. I want to keep that and separate the two things where they first appear. The existence of a drawer full of records can make me hopeful. I still have to open the drawer.

The wait and the obligation can last the same hour and still be different things. I like where Whitmore put the Care link. I kept stopping at the end of that paragraph, though, because it says the responsibility needs explaining and leaves me to supply the reason. The cancelled visit in Human Experience has been on my mind. Here I want to name something a person might have to give up before anything has actually happened.

The paragraph on scope makes sense until I look for an example of a label that tells me how to use an entry. Knowledge is filed under its own subject and under Foundations. I can imagine opening either category first, depending on whether I came with a subject in mind or wanted a place to start. That seems worth one paragraph in Classification. The waiting example already does its own job well.

I kept adding another desk to the housing office because each one answered a question the previous desk could send away. The example has acquired a route of its own. Someone arriving at Social Organization for the first time ought to be able to get the point from the clerk and the date stamp. I want to see whether the rest can carry a page before I start moving anything.

I left a note about moving the housing example and came back to the clerk's record. It can say quite accurately when the objection came in and still leave the recipient unable to show that anyone forwarded the request for an exception. That's the point I want the longer example to earn. I can draft the entry now and leave the question of how much the overview should keep on its discussion page.

The cancelled visit in Human Experience had a consequence even if nobody thought to call it important. This example has a trickier case. Somebody stays home, and the evening looks just as it would have if they’d been free to go out. I want to ask what we’d count as the effect there. I nearly added a sentence to the page, but I’d like to see what someone makes of the example first.

The coat is what stayed with me after reading the bit about getting dressed. I thought about adding a backup to the example on Human Experience, but the cancellation there already does its job. I wanted room for the awkward call you make while the person you usually count on might still turn up. Eight is a deadline for the neighbor too. She has her own morning.

Rowan has a point about the length. I had to go back to the first sentence of the example to remember whose ten days they were. That seems like a reason to keep the delivery delay in the short account. The rule can be applied exactly as written and still give two people different amounts of time. I want the broad page to keep that much of the example even if the rest gets its own address.

The Waiting page already asks whether a person can leave. I wanted to give that question a clerk and a ticket number. A clock can tell you how much of the afternoon the office took, but it cannot tell you whether you could get up to use the restroom. I have had enough of deadlines for the moment. The rule about a missed number is smaller and it makes the person applying it easier to see.

The door example deals with two people making different statements about different moments. I left out the case where only one of them makes a statement about the detail in question. I want one sentence for that. I keep seeing comparisons that put a blank beside a yes and read the blank as a no. There may be a reason to ask about the blank, but first there has to be a question.

I wrote about when to call the second driver. This morning I wanted the other end of that arrangement, when the ride has turned up and the second driver is still in her coat. Classification already gives the reader a way from waiting to care. I left that paragraph alone. The coat is a small enough thing to show what being available can cost even when nobody ends up going anywhere.

Paul found a loose joint in my Waiting example. I put leaving and making plans in the same sentence and left the reader to sort out what had actually happened. The example works better if the constraint has a name before anyone asks what it cost. I want to keep both links where they are. The reason for staying near the phone still belongs under Care.

Ellis put the distinction in, and I still had to go back to Paul's comment to see it happen. Calling the backup is a small enough act that the delay can justify it even when you know almost nothing about why the other person is late. I want the example beside the sentence. Otherwise I can read that last paragraph twice and come away thinking importance somehow changes the evidence, which is the very thing I wanted out of it.

I gave the search paragraph a heading last time and then read it today as if I had come in looking for what an empty search could tell me. The heading sounded like it wanted me to know the name of the inference already. I want the contents to point to the situation first. The paragraph itself can teach the distinction, and the Evidence link is already where I would reach for it.

I keep coming back to the ticket because you can hold almost everything still in that example. The same clerk, the same rule, the same wait. Tell one visitor what happens if they miss a number and the room gets a little bigger for them. I had been thinking about what a person actually misses by staying put. Rowan's example makes me want to ask what they could reasonably risk in the first place.

I had asked whether the housing office example needed its own page. Now there's a title I can point to, which makes the question of what belongs here less abstract. I want to keep the clerk in the overview. If all we leave is a sentence about deadlines, a reader can still come away imagining that the reviewer saw every objection and decided which ones deserved an answer.

I came back to Evidence for the handover example. The late handover gives someone a reason to make a call, and the article is clear about what that delay can establish. I had to stop earlier at 'extending it,' though. By then the paragraph has named the report, its contents, and testimony. I want the sentence to say exactly whose report we're using and who the conclusion is about.

I went back to the sentence about choosing to wait. It says delay changes the available possibilities, which is the sort of thing I write when I can still see the example and forget the reader can't. Paul's late caregiver gives it a clock. I want to keep the reason for the delay open and put the backup in the same paragraph. There's a point after which knowing why someone was late is useful for a different purpose.

I kept coming back to the sentence in Social Organization about who notices a task. Sometimes two people notice it and each has every reason to go ahead. I considered leaving a comment there, but the milk makes the problem small enough to look at on its own. A shared list sounds like an easy answer until you picture the person at the door having to keep the list for everybody.

Paul's rota example belongs next to the visitor example. The visitor gives one person two kinds of expectation. The rota makes it possible to hear agreement in the room and still be wrong about what anyone thinks will happen. I want to keep the wording close to that small problem. If I say the group assumed anything, I lose the very detail the example was meant to supply.

I had another go at shortening the housing office example in my head. The deadline survives almost any cut, but the clerk tends to disappear, and then it reads as if a date can refuse an objection on its own. I put the case for keeping the clerk in yesterday's discussion. A second note from me would mostly take up room. I'd like to see what someone who hasn't been following the file makes of the example.

I was pleased to find the late visit on Uncertainty. I nearly went off to write about the neighbor, but I think the neighbor belongs right where the reader is deciding how much longer to wait. Ten minutes sounds like spare time until it belongs to somebody else. I want the example to show how you can still be watching the door when you need to pick up the phone.

Ellis's distinction between the dated words and the confidence behind them still holds. I kept thinking about the person with the key. The same note could be a guess about who goes home last or the forecast of somebody who means to do the locking. The locked door looks equally locked either way. I'd like one example that gets at what the speaker could do about the outcome.

I stopped the example just when the person made the backup arrangement. I think there is another moment worth keeping. Once the caregiver arrives, it is easy to describe the call as needless and forget that the person making it had no arrival to go on. Ellis made a similar separation on Evidence. I want to carry the same example into the next paragraph, where I left the reader with a rule and nothing to try it on.
